1.1: 1.1 Argument. Job is said to have dwelt in the land of Ausitis, on the borders of Idumea and Arabia; and his name before was Jobab. He took an Arabian wife and begot a son, whom he named Ennon. He himself was the son of Zara, a son of the sons of Esau, and of a mother from Bosra, so that he is the fifth from Abraham. And these are the kings who reigned in Edom, in which he too reigned. But the first to reign in it was Bela, the son of Beor, and the name of that city was Denaba. After Bela came Jobab, who is called Job. After Job came Husan, who was a leader from the region of the Temanites. And after him reigned Adad, son of Badad, who cut down Midian in the plain of Moab, and the name of his city was Avith. Prologue begins. From Gregory, on Job, throughout. Some things are said here historically, and allegorically, and morally. Some cannot be taken literally, because they would be erroneous or impossible or contradictory to one another, such as: 'Under whom they stoop that bear up the world' (Job 9), as though giants carried the world; and: 'My soul has chosen hanging' (Job 7), as though one so patient wished to end his life by hanging; and: 'Let the day perish wherein I was born' (Job 3), and so on. Sometimes he who neglects the sense of the letter hides the light of truth from himself, since in seeking something within he loses what lies outside; as when, in his speaking of works of mercy, 'If I have denied to the poor what they desired' (Job 31), he looks for an allegory. For the divine word, just as it wisely exercises the learned in its mysteries, so by its surface it refreshes the simple: it is like a river both shallow and deep, in which a lamb may walk and an elephant swim. The law was given to erring man. The one disobedient to the law is put to shame by an example, above all that of a man without the law who lived lawfully. Hence Isaiah 23: 'Be ashamed, O Sidon,' that is, the steadfastness of those placed under the law, 'says the sea': the Gentile world, which, while it keeps the law, convicts the hearers of the law. Moses is said to have written these things about Job, as about one who came before; for in Genesis one reads that Jobab descended from Esau and succeeded Balak, the son of Beor, in the kingdom. But it is the custom of sacred speech, in earlier parts, to touch briefly on things that will follow long afterward, as it hastens to other matters. So Job was not before the law, but in the time of the Judges, because he himself is more truly believed to have written the deeds of his own victory. Nor does it matter that it says, 'Job said, or did these things': for it is the custom of the saints to speak of themselves as of others, for it is the Spirit who speaks in them as of others. Hence the angel of Moses is sometimes called an angel, who serves outwardly, and sometimes the Lord, who presides within; and so David: 'Attend, O my people, to my law' (Psalm 77). For the people or the law was not David's, but his who speaks in him. And he willed to be prophesied of by a Gentile as by a Jew, he who had come for both peoples. Fruitless talkativeness, like the leaves of words, is cut away by the divine, since it is forbidden that a grove be planted in the temple of God. It is unworthy that the words of the heavenly oracle be confined under the rules of Donatus. Job's virtue, great in quiet, was known to himself and to God; but when stirred by scourges, it gives off a fragrance for us like spices. Hence the faithful are also compared to a grain of mustard, which unbruised is mild, but if crushed grows fiery, and what lay hidden in it comes forth; hence in the Psalm: 'In the day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it' (Psalm 41). The gift of mercy, which is received in the quiet of the day, is said to be made manifest in the night of adversity. He is also scourged so that he might know how to give thanks amid evils, which was the one thing he certainly lacked. What the enemy therefore sought for evil, God permitted for good. And let no one think that any words of Job are to be reproved, whom God commends so highly, and in whom, as in the midst, the devil contends against God. As for his recounting his own good deeds, this is not arrogance; rather through them he strengthens himself against despair, since through so many evils and the reproaches of his friends he was being driven to despair of his life. Job is struck with every kind of temptation: with loss of goods, by which one powerful in the world was thought to be moved, but he despises these; with bereavement of children, but he grieves for this with equanimity; with the striking of his flesh, which he bears patiently; and these were like the outward assault of war, and like enemies fighting face to face. But within, through his wife, as through a fellow citizen, the mind endures the poisons of counsel, and yet he wisely instructs her too. His friends come to console, but rush forward to rebuke; among them the last and youngest rebukes more sharply, because he is unworthy; for sometimes words trouble more than wounds. Behold, as it were enemies from the flank. By wounds patience is proved; by words wisdom is exercised; the former he overcame by strength, the latter by reason. The friends of Job sinned more through ignorance than malice. For so great a man did not have wicked friends; but while they cannot discern the cause of the blows, they fall into fault. For of blows, there is one by which the wicked man is struck that he may be punished; another that he may be corrected; another lest he commit future sins; another so that, when salvation follows, the Savior may be loved the more. If a good man is struck, his merits are heaped up; not knowing how to distinguish this, they believe the one struck is struck for guilt. Hence they also the sooner return to pardon, since God humbles them here so that he might receive them to grace only through the one whom they had despised. As with all the just, so Job prefigured Christ not only in words but in deeds: so as to show, through his suffering, Christ who was to suffer, that is, the head with the body, which is the Church. His wife signifies the carnal, who within the Church, the nearer they are through faith, the more harshly they oppress life. The friends of Job signify the heretics, who under the appearance of giving counsel wish to deceive, and while they speak as if for the Lord, oppose the truth. Job means 'grieving,' by which the passion of Christ or the labor of the Church is expressed. Eliphaz: 'contempt of the Lord,' that is, heretics, who, while they think falsely about God, in their pride despise him. Baldad: 'mere antiquity,' because they speak not from good intention but from desire for glory, that is, not from zeal of the new man, but from the depravity of the old life. Sophar: 'scattering of the watchtower,' or 'scattering the watchman,' because heretics seek to strike with words the minds that contemplate the things above. In despising God, then, they keep themselves in the old state, and remaining in it they harm the watchers with evil speeches. But because they too sometimes return to the Church, the reconciliation of the friends shows this, for whom Job prays, because the sacrifices of heretics are not accepted by God unless offered by the hands of the Church. Seven sacrifices are offered for them, because when they receive the sevenfold Spirit they are, as it were, expiated by seven offerings. Bulls and rams are offered for them: in the bull the neck of pride is signified, in the ram the leadership of the flock, because, leaping away from the Church through pride, they drew weak flocks after them; and this is slain in them when they return to Job, that is, the Church. Through Elihu, who speaks with right sense but is turned aside to words of elation, one arrogant yet faithful is expressed, who is both rebuked and yet is not restored by a sacrifice, because he was overcome by the truth of faith, but displeases through the swelling of pride. Hence Elihu is interpreted 'This is my God,' or 'our God': for although proud, yet by believing truly he openly confesses, and affirms God through divinity and the Lord through the incarnation. After all his evils, he received double, because the Church here too receives double for her labors, when, having received the Gentiles, she converts the Jews also at the end, and in the future will be endowed with a double robe, that is, the blessedness of soul and body. Hence the Prophet: 'In their land they shall possess double' (Isaiah 61). It is said that Job was afflicted, but how long it lasted is passed over in silence; because the Church is known to be destined for affliction, but for how long is not known; hence: 'It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has put in his own power' (Acts 1). There was a man in the land of Hus. Gregory, on Job, vol. 1. By Job, Christ, that is, head and body, is signified: so after the history, having seen in the head what we should believe, let us see from the body what we should hold by seeing. Gregory, same place. Job in the land of Hus, etc., up to 'and the crafty things were gathered.' The same, same place. First a fitting person is described before his battle is told, so that such a one may seem able to conquer. Simple. It is necessary that the cunning of the serpent instruct the simplicity of the dove, and that simplicity temper cunning; hence: 'The Spirit appeared in a dove and in fire,' because those full of it so serve the gentleness of simplicity that they are kindled against evils with zeal for uprightness. Fearing God. Solomon: 'He who fears God neglects nothing' (Ecclesiastes 7). Same place. Likewise Solomon: 'He who offends in one thing will lose many good things' (Ecclesiastes 9). Legal animals are those that are clean according to the law, which both chew the cud and part the hoof: of these the camel has the one, but the other it lacks, and so they both agree and disagree with the law.
1.3: 1.3 Same place. And a very great household. The innumerable crowd of thoughts, which, like handmaids when the mistress, that is reason, is absent, abandon their work and clamor; but when she returns they work in silence: if we rule these well, the mind is not overcome by their multitude. Same place. Among all, that is, among the angels clinging to the rising light, we are great, as their companions. The 'eastern' are all who are in Christ through faith, of whom the Prophet says: 'The East is his name' (Zechariah 6); all of whom the God-Man surpasses.
1.4: 1.4 And they made a feast, etc. Same place. The sons make feasts, etc., up to 'because, fearful of everything, he grows numb to good works.' Through their houses, each one, etc. Through their houses, as Peter through Rome, Philip in Samaria, 'on his day,' that is, according to the measure of understanding, since Paul made one kind of instruction among the Greeks, Peter another among the Romans, though they did not differ in faith. The three sisters, that is, faith, hope, charity: the virtues invite them to everything they do, so that they may rejoice in it; they take strength as from food, while they become more confident in good works; they are made drunk as from drink after food, while they long to be steeped in the dew of contemplation. But from these very goods evils also arise, such as elation; or when joy in them comes to the mind, there is also a certain security, and from that, torpor. Therefore he adds: And when the days of the feast had gone round. To sanctify the sons after the banquet is, after the experience of the virtues, to direct the intention of the heart, and to cleanse everything that is done by strict reconsideration, lest one be deceived by the quality of an evil, so that things which are evil are thought good; or by the quantity of a good, so that it is believed sufficient when it is not perfect: but this is found better by praying than by examining. For the mind, lifted up by compunction, judges all things beneath it more surely.
1.5: 1.5 And when the days of the feast had gone round, etc. The days of the feast go round when the mysteries are accomplished by preaching; when all is done, Job offers for his sons, because Christ prayed to the Father for the apostles returning from preaching, and by sending the Holy Spirit sanctified them, cleansing whatever guilt could have been in them. Same place. He rises at dawn who has compunction, etc., up to 'which, when fulfilled, need expiation.' Same place. A holocaust is called wholly burnt, etc., up to 'before the eyes of God' up to 'let him cover it until the end of life.'
1.6: 1.6 Now on a certain day. Gregory, Morals, book 2, chapter 2. In an exordium the quality and the end of the matter are expressed; so here Job's temptation is said to begin on a day, because it is said to lead to victory, as in other cases. Now the matter is marked by the quality of the time, as that the angels appear to Abraham at midday, and Judas goes out by night. Now by place: as that weak Israel hears the law not on the mountain but below. Now by the quality of the air, as when it is said: 'It was winter,' when it is preached to those who will not believe; and 'it was cold,' when Peter's denial was impending. Now by posture of the body, as that Stephen saw Jesus standing. Same place. It is not said that anything was done before the Lord, etc., up to 'by which King Ahab is deceived, as his deserts demand.' Satan was present among them. Same place. In the day the Lord saw Satan, etc., up to 'as a blind man does not see the light by which he is illuminated.' Among them also Satan. Because he inserts himself among the good thoughts of God that come from God, in order to disturb them; but God uncovers him for us, hidden as he is. Hence it is said: 'Whence do you come?' to say which is to open his ambushes to us. I have gone round about the earth. He searches carnal hearts in order to put evil into them; he does not fly over but walks through, because he does not quickly leave the one he tempts, but lingers to impress the footprints of depravity. Against him Job is praised: 'Have you considered my servant?' whom God makes good and strengthens; he praises him as if in the ears of Satan, and so Satan rages more fiercely against him, saying: 'Does he fear God for nothing?' as if to say, why do you praise one whom you protect? He would be worthy of praise if, despising me, he stood against me by his own strength; hence he maliciously asks: but stretch out a little your hand; for while goods abound, the mind is somewhat lifted up, as though the goods were from itself; and the devil desires these goods wickedly, but God permits the testing well, so that, while man is shaken in those goods, having recognized his weakness he may be made firm in God. Hence he adds: Behold, all that he has is in your hand.
1.7: 1.7 To whom the Lord said, etc. Same place. The Lord does not, etc., up to 'which is to pant with the heat of his malice toward the affliction of the good.' Whence do you come? Gregory. He does not ask this of the good, because we ask only what we do not know, and for God not to know is to reject, as a good man too is said not to know how to lie, not that he does not know, but that he scorns it. To say, then, 'Whence do you come?' is to reject his ways as, so to speak, unknown. I have gone round about the earth. By the circuit of going round the anxiety of toil is signified. He went round the earth laboring, who did not stay quiet in heaven; and he does not fly over but walks through, because he fell from the flight of spiritual power, weighed down by the heaviness of his malice. Of his members also it is said: 'The wicked walk round about' (Psalm 11), that is, they are wearied by labor in outward things. The devil contends not against Job but, in the midst of Job, against God. Hence Job did not first ask this of God, but God praised him in his sight.
1.9: 1.9 Does Job fear God for nothing? etc. Same place. The devil had sensed that the Redeemer had come, but because of the lowly things he suffered, whatever he had suspected about his divinity came to him as a doubt, through his own pride, and he believed him not to be God born, but one guarded by God's grace. Have you not fenced? He speaks of a fenced house, because by tempting he could not penetrate its substance, because he did not presume to attack his elect. His possession has increased. Same place. As if to say: because he has received so many goods on earth, he behaves innocently for the sake of these; but he would not be innocent if he stood amid adversities; for he wishes to reprove him, who cannot be in the day, in the night of adversities. So not knowing Job's strength, but knowing more truly that each one is proved by adversities, he asks to tempt him. But stretch out, and he does not ascribe to himself the power of striking; his will is always wicked, which is from himself; the power is just, which is from God; hence: 'The evil spirit of the Lord was upon Saul,' and he is of the Lord by permission, and evil by will. Hand. Same place. He complains that the number of the faithful is increased by the preaching of the apostles: for Satan to say this is to think such things in envy and to grieve over them, wasting away.
1.11: 1.11 Touch. Same place. Because what he asks to have crushed are outward things, and he thinks it of little account unless he harm the soul. To his face. The face of the Lord is the regard of grace. He says therefore: if you withdraw the gifts he loves, he does not seek the regard, namely of your grace, your favor, but in cursing despises it.
1.12: 1.12 The Lord therefore said. Same place. God is not conquered by being provoked by the devil's petition, but grants to the enemy, for his own grief and deception, what profits the servant. Behold, all that he has, etc. By a holy dispensation he loosens and restrains: he gives up the substance, he protects the body, although he would later deliver the body too, yet not all at once, lest things heaped together destroy what, divided, can be borne. Or the Lord knew Job's lot, and yet divided the battles, that he might be the more wonderfully victorious, since the defeated enemy would repair himself again for new battles. Behold, all... only upon him, etc., that is, I grant that his goods be tested outwardly, but within I keep him for myself. But stretch out. Same place. He thought that Christ could sin through sufferings. Behold, all that he has is in your hand. The hand of Satan is not power but temptation: first Judea, which had been his possession, was taken away through unbelief and set against him; afterwards his flesh also was crucified. He went out. That is, he attained the wishes of his desire. Or he goes out when what is permitted him with good intention is carried out by him with a perverse intention. Satan went out. From where did he go out, from him who is everywhere? But as long as, held down by the power of God, Satan could not carry out what he desired, he stood, as it were, before his face; he goes out when he is loosed to the effect of his desire. And he went out from the presence. Because, while he cannot prevail as far as the heart, shut out from the inmost things he wanders outwardly; and if he disturbs the mind, he is outside, because he does not destroy but teaches. Same place. Times suit temptations. He chose a fitting time to tempt when he found his sons at a feast: the joy of satiety is a foretelling of tribulation.
7.9: 7.9 As a cloud is consumed. Same place. A cloud is lifted to the heights, etc., up to 'go to your house.'
7.10: 7.10 Nor shall his place know him any more. Same place. Man's place is God, etc., up to 'still feels contradiction from the corruption of the flesh.'
7.12: 7.12 Am I a sea? Same place. The prison is the flesh which hinders, etc., up to 'now he adds counsel against these things.'
7.15: 7.15 Wherefore my soul has chosen. Same place. The soul is the intention of the mind, etc., up to 'if you are going to do this to me, kill me.'
7.16: 7.16 Spare me, Lord, that you may give eternal things, because by contempt of these, these are better hoped for. While he asks to be spared, he proves that he has not despaired of God; what is 'he chose hanging,' that is, he despaired, he brought in concerning the same, 'spare': which is, death for the bones: that is, let them not live beyond this third time. For my days are nothing. He who considers eternal things, returning to himself, rightly calls these days nothing, and dreads being judged strictly.
7.17: 7.17 What is man? Same place. God magnifies man with much spiritual gift, and sets his heart toward him, because he judges more strictly for what is given. But what is man? As if to say: although magnified beyond himself by your gifts, yet because he is flesh, if he is judged without mercy he cannot bear it, hence he adds further:
7.18: 7.18 You visit him early in the morning. The early morning is when man comes from the night of vices and ignorance to the light, in which he is soon also tried: for lest he glory that he has good things from himself, he is permitted to be shaken by temptation, that the height of God and his own weakness may be seen, as Solomon after wisdom is tempted by harlots; man suffers all this in this mortality, hence: How long will you not spare me?
7.19: 7.19 My spittle. Same place. Spittle flows into the mouth from the head, etc., up to 'he who wishes to deserve this confesses the evil he has done': I have sinned, etc.
7.20: 7.20 I have sinned; what shall I do to you? Same place. As if to say: what to offer you in recompense I do not find, because all the strength of man is weak to wash away guilt. Or, what shall I do to you, as if to say: all goods profit not you but us. O keeper of men. Because he so leaves us destitute that we cannot guard ourselves, and if we attempt anything we are burdened with sins, hence: Why have you set me contrary to you? When man believed the serpent, etc., up to 'but seeks mercy,' hence he adds:
7.21: 7.21 Why do you not take away? Behold the desire for the Mediator, who takes away the sins of the world. Or, then sin will be fully taken away, when man will be changed into incorruption. He desires therefore the Redeemer or the resurrection, hence he adds both the penalty that he deserved from his origin and the judgment he fears from his own action. Behold, now to sinning man it was said: 'You are dust, and to dust you shall return.' Why have you set me contrary to you? Same place. Because the lower, made contrary now to the higher, that is God: therefore our lower part, that is sensuality, has been made contrary to the higher, that is the spirit, so that they always fight. In the morning, that is, at the coming of the judge, to whom all things are open. To seek of God is to judge strictly, before whom not even the just man stands; but this is the solace of deliverance, that the humble man says he cannot suffice; he laments therefore the death that now is, he fears the judgment that is impending.
8.1: 8.1 And Baldad answering. Gregory. It must be known first that, as Eliphaz chiefly charged most holy Job with pride, though he touched briefly on hypocrisy as well, so this man means chiefly to charge him with hypocrisy; but before doing this he puts forward something by which it is weighed how burdensome to him were the words of Job himself, namely words of edification: as though, unable to bear him speaking well any longer, he burst out indignantly in these words, saying:
8.2: 8.2 How long will you speak such things? As if to say: why do you speak useless things? And the spirit of your mouth is manifold. How long will you speak such things? Same place. Because the words of edification are so heavy to the wicked that he seems not able to bear them; and because he does not wish to be corrected, he accuses what is well said. And the spirit manifold. Same place. In attributing multiplicity to his speech, he rebukes his poverty of understanding. And note that there are four kinds of speaking. Some are ample in mouth and sense, who are to be praised; others narrow in both, who are to be pitied; others ample in sense but cannot express it, who are to be helped; others poor in sense but streaming in tongue, who are to be despised: this man twists into a charge against Job.
8.3: 8.3 Does God? Gregory. Job had neither denied nor been ignorant of this, etc., up to 'as if they justly perished, they strike others,' hence he adds:
8.4: 8.4 Even if your sons have sinned, etc. If at dawn: as though they are in the light, the Church in the night, whom they call to rise through knowledge of God and by the prayer of repentance wash away the past, if clean in thought, upright in work.
8.6: 8.6 He will awake. He who now sleeps from the help of you who err. And will make peaceful. Gregory. That is, he will restore the tranquillity of the present life, which alone they think to be the reward of God. The habitation of the just. Same place. They call that which is pacified the counsel of the mind, because if they draw them to their side, they fall silent from contention. They also promise riches of understanding by speaking.
8.7: 8.7 To such a degree. But because their words are not easily believed, they bend the sayings of the fathers into proof of their error, hence it is added: That the former. Because they promise that both lost things will be recovered and still greater rewards of the present life.
8.8: 8.8 For ask the former generations. They advise not to look but to investigate, because they do not want to be seen what is plainly evident to all.
8.9: 8.9 We are but of yesterday: sometimes they teach morally that the present is inferred from the past, namely from their passing that these things are nothing, hence he adds, of yesterday. Because if the former generation is recalled, this life is known to pass quickly like a shadow.
8.10: 8.10 They themselves will teach you. They praise the fathers together with us, so that he may assail us the more. Out of their heart. Same place. As if you have simplicity of spirit in the mouth, not in the heart: they the contrary. Often the wicked, not attending to themselves, tear the good, and either bring forth good things which they learned not by seeing but by hearing, or heap on others the evils which they themselves do, and so excuse themselves by deeds, judge by words. Thus Baldad, a pretender of justice, says wonderful things against hypocrites, and presumes to teach the just about what would suit the perverse. Senseless is he who pours water into a river for thirsty gardens.
8.11: 8.11 Can the rush live? Same place. He compares the hypocrite to the rush or reed-bed, etc., up to 'but would show by the crimes of others.' Before all herbs. Same place. The just are also grass according to the flesh, because 'all flesh is grass' (Isaiah 40); they wither, because their works fail with the life of the flesh. But those of hypocrites before: because they soon forsake good works as soon as they have obtained that for which they pretended. These are the grass of the roofs, which withers before it is plucked up.
8.13: 8.13 So are the ways of all. Behold to whom he compares the rush or reed: the hope of the hypocrite is glory and such worldly things, which perish; eternal things remain.
8.14: 8.14 His folly shall not please him. Same place. Folly is to sell a great thing at a low price, that is, to do laborious good deeds for favor: now he is delighted by it, but in punishment it will displease, and then he will know that all things that have passed were nothing, hence: And his confidence like a spider's web. A spider's web is carefully woven, scattered by a breath of wind: so whatever the hypocrite sweats over, the breeze of favor carries off.
8.15: 8.15 He will lean upon his house. The house of the mind is any thing in which the soul dwells by love: the house of the hypocrite, therefore, is favor. Or the house is confidence in holiness, which will stand before men but not before God.
8.16: 8.16 He seems moist. The rush, the hypocrite, seems moist in the night, that is, appears to men steeped in the grace of holiness, but before the sun on the day of judgment will wither. And in his rising a shoot. Any herb is first produced from the earth, etc., up to 'the hypocrite, even when he acts rightly, wishes to be seen by many.'
8.17: 8.17 Over a heap of stones. Same place. The roots are thoughts; the stones, because 'living' is not added, are men good and bad; the hypocrite, then, who dwells among stones, multiplies thoughts in seeking the admiration of men: for in all that he does he seeks praise by hidden thought, openly having what the enemies may plunder. As Hezekiah, who after many benefits done to him showed all his goods to the messengers of the king of Babylon: hence he soon heard: 'All shall be carried to Babylon' (2 Kings 20); so too, while praise is sought, virtue and beauty are handed over into the hands of the enemy, hence Baldad says: And he shall dwell among stones. Because he stands where he fixes the intention of his mind: and even if he be full of goods, if God swallow him up, that is, take him by death from the place, that is, from the favors of this life; he will say: 'I do not know you,' as is said to the foolish virgins (Matthew 25): and rightly, because it is not enough for him unless he has made others like himself, and this is what he says: for this is the joy of his way. This is the joy, etc. Same place. So that he may also be punished for their guilt, but:
8.20: 8.20 God will not cast away the simple. Whose simplicity is now called folly by the cunning of the double-minded. Nor will he stretch out his hand. Same place. To lift him from the depth where they seek glory. The hypocrites are malignant, who do not even do good things well. Or because they show themselves outwardly pure and simple to their neighbor, while hiding duplicity within; against whom Moses says: 'You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen' (Deuteronomy 22).
8.21: 8.21 Until your mouth be filled. Not that afterward he will not, which is evident; but 'not before,' which could seem doubtful to men: as if to say, he neither forsakes the simple before the judgment nor ceases to strike the wicked. Your mouth be filled with laughter, that is, the mind with the joy of eternal security, hence: And your lips with rejoicing. Rejoicing is conceived in the heart with such gladness as speech cannot unfold, yet the mouth sounds it.
8.22: 8.22 Those who hate you. Same place. Confusion will clothe the enemies of the just in the judgment, because then, the judge being seen, all evils are turned before the eyes of the mind, and guilt, pressing them down, clothes them on every side. They come to this because here they loved only transitory things, hence he adds: And the tabernacle, that is, the building of eternal happiness, which they multiply as though about to fall upon them, so as to defend themselves here from necessities as from heat and rain: in which the mind dwells, which the good traveler despises.
9.1: 9.1 And Job answering said. Gregory, on Job. The perverse, to whom the speaker's person is displeasing, assail all that he says, whether wrong or right; but Job, to whom the person is not displeasing but the fault, seeing that Baldad had spoken rightly: 'Does God pervert judgment?' and had brought forward true things against the hypocrites, approves what he heard. Truly I know that the humble man, subject to God, receives justice, the self-composed loses it, because he who compares himself to him, arrogating to himself what is God's, deprives himself of the good he received. But also every merit of our virtue, if judged strictly, is a vice.
9.3: 9.3 If he will contend with him, Same place. by presuming on his merits and arrogating the glory of his virtue not to God but to himself. He cannot answer him one for a thousand. Same place. That is, he will not be able himself, etc., up to 'but lest he contend, let the sight of his power terrify the weak.'
9.4: 9.4 Who has resisted him and had peace? He who creates so that created things agree with him, orders in what they may have peace, and he who tries to resist his disposition loses peace, as the angel who, lifted by his own restlessness, and man who is vexed by the trouble of the flesh, because he would not be subject to his maker; each lost peace.
9.5: 9.5 Who removed mountains, etc. Same place. Said generally for the confusion of pride, it shows in the destruction of Israel what punishment awaits the proud. He removed mountains: the holy preachers from the Jews to the Gentiles, which the Jews did not know, who were overthrown in this, thinking joy was theirs when they had lost the light. With the mountains removed, he shakes the earth.
9.6: 9.6 Who shakes the earth out of its place. Because he drew the Jews out of their borders through the Romans. The pillars: priests, princes, doctors of the law. They are shaken, because they were not allowed to live even for themselves; hence they drove out the apostles, and besides were abandoned in the darkness of their error.
9.7: 9.7 Who commands the sun. Same place. The sun shines by day, etc., up to 'is spread abroad among all nations.' Hence:
9.8: 9.8 Who alone stretches out the heavens. Same place. That is, he causes the apostles, driven out by the Jews, to be honored everywhere. Alone. Who wonderfully dispensed this, even while the bitterness of the world raged in the killing of the good. He walks upon the waves, that is, he treads them down while softening them by the wonder of signs. Jeremiah: 'I have set the sand as a boundary for the sea' (Jeremiah 5), that is, to break the glory of the world he chose the lowly and the poor; but while the sea rages, the Church advances.
9.9: 9.9 Who makes Arcturus. Same place. He uses the names of the philosophers, etc., up to 'it is turned, is raised, as Arcturus.' Orion. Same place. Which rise in winter time, etc., up to 'but raised them, calm, to their death.' Hyades. They are born in the forehead of Taurus in spring, etc., up to 'it reaches the inner things of the supernal homeland,' hence he adds: And the inner chambers of the south. The south is the fervor of the Holy Spirit, etc., up to 'comprehends better by failing,' saying:
9.10: 9.10 Who does for me. He explains better who confesses he cannot explain, and speaks more eloquently who is silent in astonishment. Great, by power. And incomprehensible, by reason. And wonders, of which there is no multitude. But why should we marvel at things that are outside us, when we do not know even what is done toward ourselves? If he come to me.
9.11: 9.11 If he come to me. Same place. He comes when he gives gifts, etc., up to 'and yet blind man will so render an account to God for his acts.'
9.12: 9.12 If suddenly he ask. Same place. He asks suddenly when the unexpected, etc., up to 'which is shown more plainly when it is added: Who can say, Why do you so?' We ought to revere the deeds of God, etc., up to 'which the proud kindles inextinguishably,' hence he says:
9.13: 9.13 God, whose wrath none can resist. Moses and Phinees and other saints, etc., up to 'returning from these to himself, humbly grows vile to himself before the power of God.'
9.14: 9.14 How great then am I. Same place. That is, if an angel is not sufficient to consider him, with what mind do I, pressed by flesh, dispute about his judgments? Our words toward God are works, but with these man cannot speak with God, because in them there is no confidence before the subtle judgment of God, hence he adds:
9.15: 9.15 Who, though I have anything, etc., I will beseech. After justice he needs prayer, that what is less by himself may be strong by the mercy of the judge. Even if justice be full in the more perfect, it is said 'to have something' of it, because the mind of man scarcely carries out what it comprehends, and what it comprehends is little. Prayer, because it is shaken by many thoughts, even if heard, fears to be repelled.
9.16: 9.16 When I have called, he will not hear me. Same place. For when, as David says, they now 'ascend to heaven' (Psalm 106), when they penetrate the highest things, now 'descend to the depths' through foul temptations, they do not have certainty of being heard. See how subtly he judges himself, reveals his weakness. How great then. He does not trust in justice but flees to prayer: who, even if I have something just, fearful even about the prayer itself says: When I have called. He looks around so carefully because he sees that he cannot bear the force of the judgment, of which he says:
9.17: 9.17 For he will crush me in a whirlwind. He who despised him when waited for in tranquillity will be crushed in a whirlwind. In a whirlwind: because in the commotion of the elements he fears that works will be strictly required there; since he sees that some are condemned without works by original guilt, in whose voice he says: He will multiply my wounds. Because they have done nothing, hence it is said: 'No one is clean in his sight, not even an infant of one day.' Without cause. According to the estimation of human sense; but with God it is just that the tree keep in its branches the bitterness it drew from the root. This also spiritually of Job, who foresaw the scourges of God in a whirlwind, and fearing, foresaw, and foreseeing, bore them, hence he says: And will multiply my wounds without cause, because he was not struck for guilt, hence above: 'that I might afflict him in vain.'
9.18: 9.18 He does not allow. Gregory. Full proof: outwardly torments tear him, within temptations chasten, hence he says he is filled with bitterness, but the equity and power of the one who strikes mitigates the force of the pain. And this is:
9.19: 9.19 If strength is sought. As if to say: no one dares, because he examines merits who does not explore them through another's testimony, but silent as a consideration waits long. Another cannot be a witness for me, because neither can I be for myself.
9.20: 9.20 If I would justify. Same place. I am not sufficient to be a witness of innocence, nor do I know that I have it.
9.21: 9.21 If I be simple. He who knows the good he does, etc., up to 'bears this exile of blindness with difficulty,' hence he adds: And it will weary me of my life. But there is consolation in this darkness when the just power of God is brought back to mind: who both punishes the wicked and surpasses the just.
9.22: 9.22 It is one thing that I have said. Same place. Or the innocent is consumed, etc., up to 'let him destroy our double nature of flesh and soul.'
9.23: 9.23 If he scourges, let him kill himself. Same place. The laughing of God is at affliction, etc., up to 'which alone bore the death of the flesh, he reveals.'
9.24: 9.24 The earth is given. Or handed over. The earth is the flesh, the wicked one the devil. His hand, the killers of Christ, etc., up to 'to which Christ will have come.'
9.25: 9.25 My days have been swifter than a runner. Same place. It belongs to a runner to announce what is to follow: so all the elect before the coming who announced Christ were runners; but because they die before, they grieve that they pass more swiftly than a runner, so as not to see him present who is singularly called good; of whom he also adds
9.26: 9.26 Like ships. He who carries apples enjoys the fragrance, etc., up to 'by compassion the speech is turned also to their hardness thus.'
9.27: 9.27 When I shall say: By no means. Same place. Israel, as before, did not wish to speak, when it denied him whom it foretold: in which his inner face is changed by the filth of unbelief so that it is not recognized by God, hence it remains to be tormented with eternal sorrows. My days have passed more swiftly. Same place. The first man was so created that his life could be extended through times, not unrolled; but because he sinned he bore a running-down, which man always endures, and yet wishes for, while he desires to live. The losses of this running-down he groans in the voice of the human race. They have fled, because man would not stand in the light, by fleeing he lost the sight, that he cannot see the good that is, for which he was made. Like ships carrying apples. Same place. The fruits of the earth through the waves, etc., up to 'which thought, lest it burst out into pride, humbly presses itself down, saying: I will by no means speak so. But being weak I shall be restrained from such inquiry.' In which the face of the mind is changed, because, seeing itself weak, it reveres what it does not know of the high things it was seeking. In which there is sorrow, because he is greatly afflicted who is blinded to understanding the things that concern himself. To these common evils he fears to add his own: I feared all, etc.
9.28: 9.28 I feared all my works. Same place. They were indeed good, etc., up to 'as if he does not come to life even through labors,' hence:
9.29: 9.29 But if I am thus also wicked. He does not repent of having labored, but amid labors grieves that he is uncertain of the rewards. The just man is so uncertain that he trusts, he so trusts that he not grow numb in security. In vain: I say that.
9.30: 9.30 If I were washed as with snow waters. He who wears himself down with laments, etc., up to 'he who is pricked in prayer for earthly things, the water of the earth.' Hands. Same place. These are works. As the cleanest, as if not truly clean under this corruption.
9.31: 9.31 You will dip, that is, you will show me dipped, because the nearer we approach him, the more we recognize our filth from his cleanness. Garments. The garment of the soul is the body, which Solomon commanded to be white at all times, and if it be mixed with blood, that is, carnal desires, Isaiah says it is to be burned (Isaiah 9). They will abominate, that is, they will make abominable, as it is said of Judas: 'He possessed a field of the reward of iniquity,' that is, caused it to be possessed. In the abomination of the garment this is the heavier, that it does not know the sense of its reprover.
9.32: 9.32 For I shall not answer a man like myself. Among men we both hear the objections and respond to them and are heard; but in the judgment of God he hears us, because he sees all we do, but we do not hear him, because we do not fully understand what displeases him. He cannot be heard on equal terms.
9.33: 9.33 Let both be able: that is, God and me: To reprove. He reproves who by the authority of reason, etc., up to 'who corrected the hearts of sinners rather by gentleness than by terror,' hence he adds:
9.34: 9.34 Let him take away from me the rod of the law with which he punishes; but Christ took it away, and by gentleness showed the ways of life. He willed to be feared as God, but loved as a father.
9.35: 9.35 I will speak and not fear him. Same place. Now he has not fear, but affection as toward a father. Behold the staff, that is, the fear of the law, sent, does not raise the boy; but Elisha himself, conforming himself to the boy and breathing seven times, that is through the love of the Spirit. Gregory. To answer is to repay with worthy deeds, but who answers the benefits of God fearing servilely? Only he who by the confidence of love does not fear that worthy services be rendered to him. He is not pure who would do evil if it were allowed. To the lover, however, there is weariness of this life, which before was sweet, even mourning he endures it.
10.1: 10.1 My soul is weary of my life. Same place. But when this life grows cheap through love of the heavenly, he who defended his faults now accuses them. And this is: I will let go the speech with which I used to defend myself. Against myself, because by confessing I accuse myself, not as one who is still ashamed to confess, because he does not forsake evils with so great a desire, but because sometimes one confessing openly does not groan but speaks rejoicing over what is to be mourned, he adds: I will speak in the bitterness, that bitterness may punish what the tongue accuses. From repentance security is born, and he more confidently asks how he is dealt with. And this is:
10.2: 10.2 I will say to God: Do not condemn me, because my penalty extinguishes your punishments. Tell me why you judge me so, that is, scourge me, whether for security or for what fault specially; because even if just, he still has some evils: and therefore he asks that God show himself to him, so that what God punishes in him he too may punish by weeping. Therefore I seek the cause; for I know that it is not unjust. Why do you judge me so? He judges here in two ways. Either he sends punishment, etc., up to 'whom even by striking he keeps in innocence.' He says therefore:
10.3: 10.3 Is it good? This question demands a denial, etc., up to 'because he considers the weak.' The work of your hands. As if to say, you do not impiously destroy him whom you made freely. Of the wicked, that is, of the malignant spirits, who, since they cannot return to life, seek companions in death, whose counsel was to break upright Job with adversities after prosperity; but God does not allow him to be tempted beyond his strength.
10.4: 10.4 Have you eyes of flesh? The eyes of flesh recognize only things done in time, because they also are closed with time, and human sight follows any work, does not run before it.
10.5: 10.5 Are your days. The days and years of man also differ from the eternal: for whom nothing passes, nothing is to come, but who sees all things as present.
10.6: 10.6 That you should inquire into my iniquity. And so you may know that I have done nothing impiously, as if humbly asking: why do you prove in time by scourges one whom you knew perfectly with yourself and before times?
10.7: 10.7 Since there is none. Same place. As if to say: what remains for you but to spare, you whom none can resist? For the more none can hold back your vengeance, the more easily piety ought to spare; and that you may be appeased, since we cannot offer our own work, let us offer him his own work.
10.8: 10.8 Your hands. As if to say: weigh mercifully, lest what you made perish. They made. According to the soul. All round about. According to the body, etc., up to 'when of the rest he said only: Let it be.' And so suddenly. As if to say, why do you despise with such vileness one whom you set above with such dignity? But with this dignity, which is by the spirit, there is weakness through the flesh, which should move the pious judge, hence he says:
10.9: 10.9 Remember, I beg, etc. Hence fault is pardonable, when it is unforgivable in the angel, who was strong. It is clay, when water pours on earth: so man, when the soul waters the flesh, whose death he openly adds: And into dust, etc. As if to say: see the material and the penalty, and spare the fault; and because he set forth the quality of man as made, he adds the order of propagation, hence he says:
10.10: 10.10 Did you not milk me out like milk, etc. Man was made like clay, but propagated like milk is drawn from the seed, curdled like cheese in the flesh. He is clothed with flesh and skin, made firm with bones and sinews. After the creation of the body, which is the lesser, there is added the wonderful breathing of vivification. Did you not, like milk, while the mind through the Spirit of God and old age is drawn like milk, because it is formed in a certain beginning; is curdled like cheese, when growing fat it is drawn together by thoughts, so that it no longer flows away in desires but is made firm in one love. But against these first elements the flesh murmurs from old custom.
10.11: 10.11 With skin and flesh. That is, the mind is hedged about by the siege of carnal movements; but he who relaxes outwardly for wars strengthens within through the bones of the virtues, so that one may be humble and strong. And God therefore bestows the uprightness of right living, because he spares past offenses.
10.12: 10.12 Life and mercy. Same place. But he gave these goods in vain unless he himself guard them, hence he adds: And your visitation. The same of the inner man, etc., up to 'thinks more subtly about the gifts of God.' Life and mercy. Same place. Life is given with evil minds, etc., up to 'after he spoke of himself, he adds generally the gifts of mercy:'
10.13: 10.13 Yet I know that you remember all things, which is said: why do I tremble for myself, who know that all nations are to be gathered? Although you hide these things in your heart. Same place. Because as yet you do not declare it in open speech. Those sure of pardon are usually touched by the memory of former wickedness, and, unwilling to be assailed by unlawful thought, hence he adds:
10.14: 10.14 If I have sinned. God spares for an hour, etc., up to 'but, struck, they fix their hope more firmly in the help of God alone.'
10.16: 10.16 Because of pride. Gregory. The lioness, while she greedily seeks food for her cubs, etc., up to 'but if we grow numb from holy desire, he sets before us the examples of those who watch well.'
10.17: 10.17 You multiply your wrath against me, that is, you show it manifold, because if he scourges the good, what will it be for the wicked? Thus, the manifold wrath being foreseen, man returns to himself and punishes perverse things.
10.19: 10.19 I should have been as though I had not been, from the womb. Same place. The same as what was said there: 'like an untimely birth hidden,' etc., or, those conceived who have not seen the light.
10.20: 10.20 Are not the days of my life few? Same place. Let not the delight of the present life take hold of me, because it quickly passes. Let me alone, then... my sorrow. Same place. That is, temper the scourges, etc., up to 'which the foreseeing of hell chiefly does,' hence he says:
10.21: 10.21 Before I go. Hell is called a land, because captives are held there. Before I go. Not that he who laments goes, but that he goes who does not lament: as if I should say to a debtor, pay before I bind you. I shall not return. Same place. Because mercy no longer frees the damned.
10.22: 10.22 Of misery and darkness. Because outwardly pain tortures those whom blindness of mind darkens within; or, there no one returns any more to the light, as in this life: where, though there be misery, one may return to the light through conversion. The shadow of death. Death is separation from God; its shadow, obscurity; because penal fire has burning and not light, so that those who sinned in both are punished in both. No order. Same place. Not that God does not order, up to 'the quality of things is not kept.' Hence he adds: Everlasting horror. This is the fear of future evil, etc., up to 'lest those come to torments whom he who saw Lazarus would see in punishment.'
11.2: 11.2 Shall he that speaks much? Gregory, on Job, book 10. He begins with insults, etc., up to 'who think nothing right except what they feel.' Or a verbose man. A true saying, because it is read that the cult of justice is silence, but not said in its proper place. He who cannot bear right things, neglecting to be corrected, girds himself for reply.
11.3: 11.3 To you alone men will be silent, etc. Same place. He whom conscience bites thinks all right things said to be mockery of himself and supposes generally spoken things to be about himself. Hence he is also kindled to speak against, so that thus at least he may govern his shame, as though he were not guilty if he accuses others, hence by lying he adds:
11.4: 11.4 For you have said: My speech is pure. Job had not said it; but it is a solace to wrongdoing if the life of the one reproving is stained even falsely.
11.5: 11.5 And oh that God would speak with you, etc. Same place. The perverse wish good things in words so as to seem kind, and so that what is present may be shown to be evil, hence he too says: Oh that God would speak. As if he said, you now speak to yourself, while you savor carnally: you are empty of the spirit of truth; as if I rather pity your inexperience than your punishment. Same place. Lips, that is, judgments, through which, opened, etc., up to 'he recognizes before God: and if he recognizes sins, he patiently bears the scourges.' And this is:
11.6: 11.6 And you would understand that many things are less. He unjustly charges the just man with iniquity, but this insult comes forth from zeal for God, and is venial. Not knowing the merits of the just man either, from inexperience he adds mockery:
11.7: 11.7 Perhaps you will comprehend the footsteps of God. Same place. The kindness of visitation, etc., up to 'because his essence will be fully seen by none.'
11.8: 11.8 Higher. Because in the circumscription of his spirit he transcends all. Deeper than hell. Because by transcending he bears up from beneath.
11.9: 11.9 Longer than the earth. Because he exceeds the measure of the creature by the perpetuity of eternity. Broader than the sea. Because he so possesses the times, etc., up to 'or do you not know how to reprove yourself in temptations?'
11.10: 11.10 If he overturn. Same place. He overturns heaven, etc., up to 'that the resisting may be exercised, or the seduced broken,' hence he rightly says: Who shall gainsay him? or, who can say to him, Why do you so? Because none can withstand the judgment of God, or penetrate it by inquiring. Why does he overturn or restrain?
11.11: 11.11 For he knows. Same place. While the mind is lifted up by elation, etc., up to 'by which vanity with iniquity draws on, namely to swelling,' he adds:
11.12: 11.12 A vain man is lifted up into pride. Same place. The vain man becomes bold from guilt, etc., up to 'through unbridled freedom, boldly wandering, runs through desires.'
11.13: 11.13 But you have hardened. Same place. The heart is hardened not in this place, etc., up to 'he adds this as if by teaching: and you shall be steadfast,' etc.
11.14: 11.14 If iniquity. Same place. Iniquity in the hand, etc., up to 'if the conscience of its guilt accuses.'
11.15: 11.15 And you shall be steadfast. Because he trembles at the judgment the less, the more firmly he stands in good acts.
11.16: 11.16 Of misery also. Same place. The mind feels the evils of the present life the more heavily, the more it neglects to weigh the good that follows. But if it fixes the eye of the heart on those things that remain, it sees that whatever tends to an end is nothing. And like waters. Because miseries that pass do not shake with force, but pour in a touch of sorrow, while outwardly one grieves at the stroke, inwardly cools from temptation, against which the divine light is the more kindled, hence it is added.
11.17: 11.17 And as the noonday. The brightness of noonday in the evening is the renewal of virtue in temptation. And when you think yourself consumed. Gregory. When the just man too has begun to succumb through outward evils, then his brightness begins: on the contrary, the light of the wicked is in the day of this life, darkness in the evening. And when you think yourself consumed. Because falling outwardly he is renewed within, and the harder things he bears, the more surely he hopes for rewards, and this is:
11.18: 11.18 And you shall have confidence. Those buried sleep securely, etc., up to 'he sleeps securely with himself, hidden from the acts of the world.'
11.19: 11.19 You shall rest and there shall be none. For he who is fixed in the desire of eternity, while there is nothing in the world he longs for, has nothing to fear from the world. And they shall entreat. The perverse, when they preach right things, promise others as great what they themselves long for; but lest by long promising what they are be laid bare, they return the sooner to words of uprightness, hence it is added:
11.20: 11.20 But the eyes of the wicked. By the name of eyes, etc., up to 'he finds nowhere to hide himself.' And their hope is abomination, etc. Same place. Because from this the spirit perishes forever, whence for a time the flesh lives sweetly.
12.1: 12.1 And Job answering. Gregory. Sophar said this truly, etc., up to 'hence Job adds:'
12.2: 12.2 Are you then the only men? He who thinks he surpasses all in reason exults to be the only man. Are you then the only men? For he who thinks himself alone to be wise, what else does he think than that this same wisdom dies with him?
12.3: 12.3 And I have a heart as well as you. To correct their pride, he denies that he is inferior; and lest he pass the limit of his humility, he is silent about being superior. See how discreetly, in which he indicates what they ought to think of themselves. For who does not know these things which you know? As if he said: Since what you say is known to all, why do you swell singularly over the knowledge of what you have said?
12.4: 12.4 He who is mocked. Same place. Because human derision makes him near to God whom the innocence of life keeps aloof from human perversities.
12.5: 12.5 A lamp despised. Same place. By the name of the rich he designates the elation of the proud; but the simplicity of the just man is called both a lamp and despised: a lamp, because it shines within; despised, because among the minds of the carnal it is reckoned base. Prepared for the appointed time. The appointed time of the despised lamp is the predestined day of the last judgment, on which it is shown with how great power each just man who is now despised shines.
12.6: 12.6 The tabernacles of robbers abound. Same place. He shows that the riches of the present life are nothing, etc., up to 'and yet the goods they have they received from God.' Ask the beasts, etc. Same place. The beasts are the duller in sense. The birds of the air are the lofty, the wise.
12.8: 12.8 The fishes. Same place. The curious are understood. And the sense is: if you ask these, they confess God as creator of all. It can also be understood according to the letter.
12.10: 12.10 In whose hand is the soul. In this place the soul of every living thing signifies the very life of the body. The spirit of all flesh. Same place. That is, the effect of man's spiritual understanding, which is in the power of God. By the soul of every living thing the life of beasts can also be signified.
12.11: 12.11 Does not the ear discern words? From these bodily things, etc., up to 'and what you know, to me through inmost love is savory to the very marrow.'
12.13: 12.13 With him is wisdom, etc. Gregory, on Job, book 21. For with God, in the beginning, was the Word, who is both the power of God and the wisdom of God; he has counsel, because he disposes his own things; understanding, because he knows ours.
12.14: 12.14 If he pull down, there is none to build. The Almighty pulls down the human race when he leaves it, builds when he fills it: unless this is done, the preacher admonishes outwardly in vain. If he shut up a man. Every man by that, etc., up to 'and not to soften the reprobate heart through grace.'
12.15: 12.15 If he hold back the waters, all things shall be dried up. Because if the knowledge of the preachers is withdrawn, etc., up to 'he related the sevenfold grace.' If he send them out, they shall overturn. For if the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured in, etc., up to 'at once the earth is overturned': because the hardness of the sinful mind is changed from the obstinacy of its immobility.
12.16: 12.16 With him is strength. In the former words in which he says, etc., up to 'he will judge how the wisdom of the Father is among the elect in the kingdom.' He knows both the deceiver and him who is deceived. Same place. He knows the deceiver, etc., up to 'it is usually at times the beginning of vengeance.'
12.17: 12.17 He leads counselors to a foolish end. By counselors he means preachers, who give counsel of life to hearers. When these preach for the sake of temporal things, they are led to a foolish end: because they strive by labor toward the place from which they should flee by uprightness of mind. And judges. Those who preside over examining the morals of others are rightly called judges; but when they by no means examine them carefully, nor know how to correct, they are led into stupor.
12.18: 12.18 He looses the belt of kings. For in those who seemed to rule their members well, on account of the fault of elation he destroys the girdle of chastity. And because in the loins is the delight of the flesh, with the cord of sin and delight he girds their loins.
12.19: 12.19 He leads priests away without glory. Same place. Because before the judge they will not find the glory which now in the morals of their subjects they do not seek with zeal of preaching. And he overthrows the nobles. Gregory. Because, when by just judgment he forsakes the mind of the rulers, they neglect heavenly things and fall here in their pleasures.
12.20: 12.20 Changing the lip of the truthful. Because often those who were truthful in preaching heavenly things, while they love temporal things, fall to loving earthly things, and the lip of the truthful is changed. Or it can be understood of the Jews, who earlier, truthful, announced that Christ would come, and denied him when present. And doctrine. Same place. The doctrine of the elders was taken away, because the Jews in no way followed by believing what they remembered their fathers had foretold.
12.21: 12.21 He pours contempt upon princes. The Jews, remaining in the commandments of the law, seemed to rule through faith; the Gentiles, pressed down in the depth through unbelief, lay hidden; but when Judea denied the mystery of the Lord's incarnation, the Gentile world believed. So:
12.22: 12.22 He reveals deep things out of darkness; when the mystical senses of allegories are recognized in the hidden words of the prophets. And brings out the shadow of death into light. Same place. He says the shadow of death, etc., up to 'the death of the flesh is least feared.'
12.23: 12.23 He multiplies the nations. Same place. Because he both extends the nations by the fruitfulness of offspring and yet leaves them in their own unbelief, and those he had left in the fall of unbelief he at length brings back to faith, and when they are thus restored, what follows comes to pass: he who changes the heart, etc.
12.24: 12.24 He who changes the heart of the princes. Same place. The heart of the princes of the earth was changed, etc., up to 'a way could not lie open against the author of all.'
12.25: 12.25 They shall grope as in the dark. Same place. For he gropes as in the dark, etc., up to 'Is not this the carpenter's son?'
13.1: 13.1 Behold, all. Gregory. For all these things to the blessed, etc., up to 'he saw some things to be in works, others in sayings,' there follows: My eye has seen these things, and my ear has heard them. But because words have no benefit if they lack understanding, there follows: And I have understood each one. For when something is shown or heard, if understanding is not given, it is not prophecy at all; and that he is not lifted up by this understanding, he shows when he says:
13.2: 13.2 According to true knowledge. By these words it became known how great his humility was, for he denies he is inferior to those whose life he had far surpassed by living holily: and he affirms that he knows according to their knowledge, he who by knowing heavenly things passed beyond their earthly thoughts through the spirit of prophecy.
13.3: 13.3 But yet I will speak to the Almighty. Same place. We speak with the Almighty when we entreat his mercy. We dispute with him when, joining ourselves to his justice, we examine our deeds with subtle inquiry. Or he disputes with God who here obeys him, and afterward will judge peoples with him, who even meanwhile does not cease to judge the wicked.
13.4: 13.4 First I will show you, etc. Same place. So the Church of the heretics: first I will show you to be fabricators; for as a building is made of stones, so a lie is fabricated of words.
13.5: 13.5 And would that you were silent. Same place. Seeing them wish to appear, etc., up to 'by which they seduce weak minds.'
13.6: 13.6 Hear therefore my correction. Same place. He rightly brought in correction first, judgment after, because unless the swelling of the fool is first depressed by correction, the judgment of the just is by no means known through understanding.
13.9: 13.9 He will be deceived as a man by your frauds. Heretics offer fraud to God who assert things which do not please him for whom they speak, and offend him while they strive to defend him.
13.10: 13.10 He will himself reprove you, because. There are those who feel the truth of God in the heart, etc., up to 'the more in the secret of thought they recognize the right judgments of God.'
13.11: 13.11 Immediately. Same place. In human speech, the movement of God means the very strictness of his rightness, which will trouble by vengeance the reprobate who here will not be troubled by repentance. And his terror shall fall upon you. Because for the reprobate fear does not bring rest, but punishment brings fear, hence the prophet: 'Vexation alone shall give understanding to the hearing' (Isaiah 28): because when they are punished for the commands of God despised, then they understand what they heard.
13.12: 13.12 Your memory. However much one for memory, etc., up to 'and the exalted flesh wastes away in rottenness.'
13.13: 13.13 Be silent a little that I may speak. He shows that they spoke by the sense of the flesh: and so he restrains them to silence, that he may say what the mind suggests to him. As if he said: I do not speak carnally but spiritually, because I hear by the sense of the spirit what I bring forth through the ministry of the body.
13.14: 13.14 Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth? The teeth in this place signify the inner senses, etc., up to 'if I cannot profit my spectators, that is, you.' With my teeth. The teeth are the inner senses, which inquire into each thing, etc., up to 'lest it be able to chew spiritual things.' And I carry my soul in my hands. Same place. To carry the soul in the hands is to show the intention of the heart in operation, which is done for the edification of the neighbor. And the sense is: Why do I either strictly judge myself before men, or show what I seek in work, if I do not profit my neighbors, neither by judging evils nor by showing goods?
13.15: 13.15 Even if he kill me, I will hope in him, etc. Same place. He is truly patient who is both worn down by adversities and yet is not bent from the uprightness of hope. Yet I will argue my ways. For so the Lord Savior will then be found, if now, for the fear of the Lord, your sin is rebuked by yourselves.
13.16: 13.16 For no hypocrite shall come into his sight. He will indeed now come before the tribunal of the judge, etc., up to 'he refuses to come in the sight of the Lord.'
13.17: 13.17 Hear my speech. By naming riddles he shows that he has figurative sayings, hence in the voice of the faithful people he adds:
13.18: 13.18 If I am judged, I know that I shall be found just, which does not differ from his person, etc., up to 'he does not ignore that he has been made just by gift.'
13.19: 13.19 Who is he that will plead with me? Because in outward acts he has nothing for which to be reproved, he freely seeks an accuser. But because the hearts even of the just reprove themselves for foolish thought, it is added: Why am I consumed in silence? As if he said: As I have lived so as to fear no accuser outwardly, would that I had so lived as not to fear an accusing conscience within me. For he is consumed in silence who finds within himself that by which he burns.
13.20: 13.20 Only two things do not to me. And the face of God here he calls his chastisement, in which, while he looks upon sins, he punishes, from which none is hidden unless the two things he asks are removed, of which follows:
13.21: 13.21 Withdraw your hand far from me. By the hand, which he asks to be made far, etc., up to 'but serves through dread.'
13.22: 13.22 Call. Gregory. He seeks the presence of Christ, that through it he may both hear what he does not know and be heard in what he knows. Or, God calls by choosing, man answers by obeying; man speaks by desiring, God answers by appearing. But so panting, he examines himself more subtly. Call me and I will answer you. God's calling is to regard us by loving and choosing. Our answering is to obey his love by good works. Or else I will speak. We speak when we ask his face through desire: he answers those who speak when he appears to us who love him.
13.23: 13.23 How many iniquities have I, etc. The labor of the just is to find themselves, and finding to lead themselves to better things by weeping and correcting. Iniquity seems graver than sin, wickedness than offense.
13.24: 13.24 Why do you hide your face? Same place. Man had the contemplation of God in paradise, but through guilt ran into darkness. And, roused by the punishment, he returns to love, and says: And do you think. Because if you looked upon me as a friend, you would not deprive me of the light of your vision.
13.25: 13.25 Against a leaf, etc. Man is called a leaf, etc., up to 'whom you recognize to be so weak?'
13.26: 13.26 You write. Because what we speak passes, what we write remains. God is said not to speak but to write bitter things when his scourges long endure over us. For he once fixed a sentence on the mortality of the flesh, which will not be able to be changed to the last. And to consume. It is clear that the sins of the young and the old are grave, if the just so fear that which they committed in a weak age.
13.27: 13.27 You have put my foot in the stocks. God put man's foot in the stocks, because he bound his perversity with the strong sentence of his strictness. And you have observed all my paths. A path is narrower than a way; since we take ways as actions, by right we take paths as the thoughts of actions. And you have considered the steps of my feet. He called the intentions of works the steps; or, perverse works, which when we do them we offer to brothers watching an evil example, and leave twisted footprints for those following, as with the foot bent out of the way.
13.28: 13.28 Who am like rottenness. As a garment is eaten by a moth that has arisen from itself, so man has in himself the rottenness by which he is consumed. Or he is tempted from the corruption of his own flesh, as a garment is consumed by a moth that has arisen. How many iniquities have I. Same place. As if man, because of the blindness of exile, does not know himself, which happens because he hides himself from the face of God, which he now grieves for, admonished by the punishment itself. Against a leaf. Man was a tree in creation, but withered in temptation to a leaf, to stubble in his casting down. You wish to consume me, because he finds he sinned in youth, etc., up to 'as if they were then indiscreet.'
14.1: 14.1 Man born of woman. Gregory. Here weakness is designated by the name of woman, and the sense is: What strength has he in himself who is born of weakness, who is both narrowed to life and widened to misery?
14.2: 14.2 Who comes forth like a flower. Because he shines in the flesh: He is crushed, because he is reduced to dust and rottenness. And flees as a shadow. He compared man not to something fleeing but to a shadow. For he who has not the warmth of heart in the love of God, and yet does not hold the life he loves, flees like a shadow. And never continues in the same state, etc. Same place. For he always fails from the very thing by which he believes he is advancing in the span of life.
14.3: 14.3 And do you think it worthy, etc. For God to open his eyes is to exercise judgments, and to see whom he strikes
14.4: 14.4 Who can make, etc. For he who alone by himself is clean, etc., up to 'he says Christ alone was not born of unclean seed.'
14.5: 14.5 The days of man are short, etc. Same place, because with God even things that glide by stand: he affirms the number of months to be with him. Or, in days the brevity of time, in months the multiplied spaces of days are designated: for man the days are short; but because our life is extended afterward, the number of our months is said to be with God. You have appointed his bounds. Gregory, on Job, book 12. For nothing that happens to men in this world happens without the hidden judgment of God.
14.6: 14.6 Depart from him a little. Depart, that is, now withdraw the scourges of the present life, and show the goods of eternal rest Until the desired day come, when he receives eternal rest in recompense for his labor
14.7: 14.7 A tree has hope, etc. He hints at the human race as if despised, and how much even the senseless things seem to precede it. Or according to the mystical sense: the tree is preferred to man, for here 'man' is any carnal one; the tree is taken as the just man, who when afflicted with the suffering of death is restored by the greenness of eternal life. And its branches sprout, because from the suffering of the just the faithful receive the greenness of spiritual life.
14.8: 14.8 If its root grow old in the earth. Same place. The root of the just man is holy preaching, because from it he arises and in it subsists: which in the hearts of earthly men is believed spent in all its strength: And its stump die in the dust, because among the hands of persecutors his body is put to death.
14.9: 14.9 At the scent of water it will bud, etc. Because by the breath of the Spirit, in the hearts of the elect, by the example of his work, he makes the shoot of virtue. And will make boughs, etc. To make boughs on a cut-down stump, etc., up to 'he made boughs, because the apostles who had withered to the faith flourished as before.'
14.10: 14.10 But man when he is dead. Same place. By the very loss of justice man dies, is stripped of the garment of innocence granted in paradise, and is consumed by the ruin of the flesh that follows: where then is he who is not in love of him, where is true being?
14.11: 14.11 As if the waters should depart from the sea. The sea is the mind of man, etc., up to 'now we are filled with the sweetness of prosperity.'
14.12: 14.12 Till the heavens be broken he shall not awake. Because, unless the end of this world comes, the human race will not awake from sleep.
14.13: 14.13 Who will grant me this? Knowing that before the coming of the Mediator he descends to hell, he asks there the protection of the Creator. Appoint me a time in which you will remember me. He asks for the coming of the Redeemer to the dead.
14.14: 14.14 Shall a dead man, do you think, live again? Just men are wont, etc., up to 'that afterward he may strengthen more.' All the days. He who therefore awaits his change with so great a desire shows how certain he is of the resurrection.
14.15: 14.15 You shall call me and I will answer. Then we truly answer God who calls when at the command of the highest incorruption we rise incorruptible. You will stretch out your right hand to the work of your hands, as if to say: therefore the corruptible creature will be able to continue to incorruption, because it will be raised by the hand of your power; or the right hand is called the Son, who incarnate was sent to raise man.
14.16: 14.16 You indeed number my steps, etc. He numbers the steps and spares sins: he who considers our deeds subtly and yet here mercifully relaxes for the penitent. You have numbered, but spare. He numbers, while he turns us to weep over each thing we have done; he spares, because he does not punish what we have punished, hence he adds still:
14.17: 14.17 You have sealed up as in a bag, etc. Same place. In secret, etc., up to 'he cares, because here through scourges he relaxes thoroughly.'
14.18: 14.18 A falling mountain comes to nothing. Same place. There are two kinds of temptations, etc., up to 'or long and slow, as you allow Solomon to be consumed.' The rock, that is, the mind of the just man, is carried From its place, that is, from justice to guilt by too great an impulse.
14.19: 14.19 Stones, that is, strength, the constant flatteries of water. The earth, which sanctifies.
14.20: 14.20 You have strengthened him for a little, etc. Same place. Man has been strengthened for a little, because here he received strength for living for a short time; but in this brevity where he was strengthened, he gathers what he may find in perpetuity; either that he may rejoice forever, or that he may not escape the punishments. You will change his face and send him away. The face of man, etc., up to 'unwilling, he is forced to pass to eternal things.'
14.21: 14.21 Whether his sons be noble. For as those still living do not know in what place the souls of the dead are held, so the carnally dead do not know how the life of those placed in the flesh is disposed after them.
14.22: 14.22 But yet his flesh while he lives shall have pain. For the tribulation of the flesh is suffered here even by those who live spiritually. And his soul over. For it is fitting that man always find sorrows in himself, who, forsaking the Creator, sought joy in himself.
15.2: 15.2 Will a wise man answer? Gregory. All that is felt in the saints displeases the wicked as if uttered to the wind, nor do they regard the words of the good as words of reason, but as goads of fury. And will fill with burning. Same place. They who say with insult what they feel also take care to cloak it with a defense of the Lord, hence he adds:
15.3: 15.3 You reprove him with words. Same place. And they think no one has the fear of the Lord except the one they have drawn to the folly of their own profession, hence he adds:
15.4: 15.4 As much as in you lies, etc., it is said, that is, you have taken away. As if he said: presuming on your justice, you scorn to beseech the grace of your Creator. When heretics do not find real evils against the good, they invent things to charge, that the just may seem guilty.
15.5: 15.5 For iniquity has taught your mouth. Gregory. Iniquity teaches the mouth when it is conceived from a bad life, what worse may be said. You imitate the tongue of blasphemers. Same place. Heretics, as though venerating God, deny lowly things, such as the flesh and death, and say that the Church confessing these things blasphemes: and if anything adverse befalls her, they say it happens for this wrong, hence he says:
15.6: 15.6 Your own mouth shall condemn you, etc. Sometimes they wish to press as if by reasoning, hence:
15.7: 15.7 Are you the first man? This defense of God is taken up by them for this reason, etc., up to 'weigh what counsel you do not know.'
15.9: 15.9 What do you know? Same place. These words plainly show from what elation of mind comes whatever sounds like a defense of the Lord.
15.10: 15.10 Both the aged and the ancient. Heretics, because they cannot support their own views by reason, try to defend them among the foolish by the authority of the ancients: and they say the doctors of the Church were their masters.
15.11: 15.11 Is it a great thing? There follows: Why does your heart lift you up? Often the mind of the just is suspended to contemplate higher things, so that outwardly their face seems stunned. But the reprobate think this force of contemplation to be done through hypocrisy; for what is in themselves they suppose in others.
15.13: 15.13 Why does your spirit swell against God? For the most part the just, afflicted by certain necessities, are compelled to declare their works, which blessed Job had done, which is thought to be elation; but proud things are not in the ears of God which are uttered with a humble heart; and as it is a grave fault to arrogate to oneself what is not, so for the most part it is no fault if one humbly says the good that is. Such words. Same place.
