Or they are wrapped, who, although at times, one wickedness being conquered, they lift the foot, another reigning entangles them also in the one they had conquered, so that he who, avarice already scorned, is still luxurious, returns to avarice for the price of luxury. Thus by alternating work the vices hold their fugitive, and bind his going out as with snares, hence they often fall back and return to their pleasures, and do not care for the things that remain, hence he adds: They shall walk in vain and perish. Because they carry nothing with them from the fruit of their labor. But the just man does not appear empty in the sight of the Lord: for he carries the sheaves of justice. From the imitation of those he frightens by the end: Consider the paths, etc.
6.19: 6.19 Consider the paths. Same place. Thema is interpreted 'south wind,' Saba 'net.' The south wind, which loosens the limbs with warmth, is here the lax relaxation of living; the net is the entanglement of action, and a man is entangled by lax actions, while he does not perfectly forsake the world, while he walks not with strict zeal but with loosened steps, as one who, out of carnal love for his parents, is hindered from the things that are God's. Consider, he says, because we love to do perverse things, but when we see them in others we judge them, and so, returning to ourselves, we blush at such things. Wait a little. Because whatever ends is little; but he who thinks this long does not care for eternal things. Having spoken of the brevity of life, he rises against the wicked with the voice of the just.
6.20: 6.20 They are confounded. Because, namely, the wicked try to draw the good back from hope through hardships; if they accomplish it they exult; if not, they blush to have been cruel in vain; hence he adds what happens in the retribution: They also came. At the judgment the wicked come to the just, because they will see their glory, so that they grieve the more heavily seeing what they have lost. Then shame covers them, when conscience as a witness burns. The same spiritually. The friends of Job were confounded, because, while they cannot bend him to despair, they are put to shame; they came when they now recognize the constancy of his mind within and blush. He shows them to be of the number of those who do not fear God except when terrified by their own or others' adversities.
6.21: 6.21 Now you have come, and now seeing my wound. Same place. As if to say: I feared God even before adversities; you, who do not fear God out of love, are afraid only of the lash.
6.22: 6.22 Did I say? The Church does not need the substance of the heretics, whose figure is the friends of Job, that is, carnal wisdom; and she refuses to hear from them the right things which they sometimes say against the devil about conversion, because through these they draw to unfaithfulness. The hand of the enemy is the strength of Satan. The malignant spirits are robust. Did I say: Bring? Against the rich of the world, etc., up to 'and what they despise in themselves, and in others.'
6.24: 6.24 Teach me. This is either joined to what precedes, or is said by itself by way of rebuke.
6.25: 6.25 Why have you detracted? Gregory. He ought to be clean, etc., up to 'do you bring forth things worthy of reproach in order to rebuke?' Same place. Two kinds of speech are harmful: that which both praises perverse things and that which also condemns right ones; there is favor, here anger: of this he accuses the friends of Job; and this vice is reached from idle words, hence he adds:
6.26: 6.26 And into the wind. To utter words into the wind, etc., up to 'let there therefore be a door of the tongue, which is now shut, now opened.'
6.27: 6.27 Upon the fatherless. Gregory, on Job, book 8. Behold, of how great weakness he judges himself to be, etc., up to 'if he tolerates those he does not love, or if he does not tolerate those he loves.'
6.28: 6.28 See whether I lie. Same place. Because, being humble, what he says he does not command by authority but persuades by reason; but because on the occasion of reason opponents are let loose to contention, he adds.
6.29: 6.29 Answer, I beg you, without contention. Because heretics in their inquiries do not aim to attain the truth but to appear victors. And speaking, etc. Because he who speaks is subject to the judgment of the hearer. Let there be an equitable arbiter between his heart and his tongue, so that nothing rushes from the heart through the tongue, but is examined before it is said. And because those who first judge their own words rightly judge the words of others, he adds:
6.30: 6.30 And you will not find in my tongue. Because folly does not sound in me to you, if it does not proceed from your own conscience; so the Church first destroys the falsehoods of enemies, and afterward opens the true things, for which there is no place while falsehoods are held for true; open speech is through the tongue, hidden consideration through the throat, because what the Church preaches outwardly she keeps by living.
7.1: 7.1 And like the days of a hireling. Gregory. He who wishes the days to pass quickly so as to come to the reward of his labor, so is every just man; and as that man sweats in another's labors but prepares his own reward for himself, so let the just man sweat in worldly evils to obtain heavenly goods. He takes care that no day go by empty of work, and the reward be lessened. He suffers hard things so as to be the more crowned, although the wage is already in his heart; yet the heat is felt more heavily in the body, so that afterward there may be refreshment in rest, and this is:
7.2: 7.2 As a servant. Rightly every elect is called a servant, as long as he is under the yoke of this corruption, before he comes into the freedom of glory. And as a hireling. He who would be provoked by the heaviness of the work if he were not relieved by hope of its end, but, that being seen, thinks nothing of what he feels.
7.3: 7.3 Empty months. Of the things of the world, because the good do not seek them by their acts, and they bear laborious nights of adversities, when they are already in the torment of the body. Or empty months, because now there is labor but not yet reward. Laborious nights. He enumerates, etc., up to 'so much the more he groans that he long did not know what he seeks, and that he labored in vain.'
7.4: 7.4 If I lie down to sleep. Same place. According to the history, the mind of one in grief is expressed, who, urged by sadness, wanders through diverse desires; in the night he longs for day, in the day for evening, because sorrow does not let what is present please; and having now found this heavy, consoled by desire he awaits another; but not even so does the sorrow end, hence: And I shall be filled with sorrows. And the cause of the sorrow is this:
7.5: 7.5 My flesh is clothed. Same place. The same more subtly in the Church, etc., up to 'for them salvation is not whole here,' hence he adds: And I shall be filled with sorrows until darkness. Because he does not find security until he wholly leaves the time of temptation. He adds the cause of the sorrow: My flesh is clothed, that is, the carnal life I lead is either polluted by evil working, or, drawn in by it, is darkened by the memory of images of sins, which rise like dust before the eyes. The Church indeed feels the rottenness of the luxury of the flesh in some, among whom, those given to earthly acts, she is sprinkled with dust; of both he adds: My skin. The skin in the Church are those who give themselves only to outward cares: whose hearts despair dries up, and therefore they are drawn together, not stretched by longsuffering toward eternal life: they cling to present things; and this happens because they do not attend how fleeting this life is. But the Church on the contrary:
7.6: 7.6 My days have passed more swiftly. As a web by its threads, so life advances by single days; but the more it grows, the nearer it tends to being cut. The speed of life, which is always failing, even surpasses the haste of the web. And therefore the elect do not fix their heart in it, hence he says: And they are consumed, that is, I put no trust in them: which the reprobate do, I do not.
7.7: 7.7 Remember. Same place. That is, kindly look upon me who am swiftly passing, because the consideration of human brevity is an acceptable offering to God. For my life is wind. Eternal life is solid: this life is judged neither solid nor lasting. Same place. And because after life passes there is no place for earning pardon, he adds: And it shall not return. That is, after death the mind, seeing its retribution, is not recalled to perform good works: hence the rich man, despairing of himself, which is an aggravation of punishment, intercedes for his brothers. Behold, life passes, what follows remains. Afterward also,
7.8: 7.8 Nor shall the eye of man behold me. That is, the mercy of the Redeemer, which softens the hardness of sinners, as when he looked at Peter (Luke 22); but after death he does not free the one whom grace did not reform before. Not the eye of man, but, Your eyes upon. Gregory. That is, you will see the strict judge ready to strike, and he who was waited for here unto repentance will no longer stand. This befits the just man, who fears everything he does, and foreknows that, piety being removed, he will perish, and does not stand before his eyes, because life does not suffice for the penalty if justice presses him. For not even the stars, that is, those who shine with holiness, are clean before him. The guilt and penalty of the human race is briefly added.
18.9: 18.9 His foot shall be held fast, etc. Namely, because his end will be bound up in sin. And thirst shall burn against him. Because the more he judges himself bound to evils, the more he despairs of his return; and by that very despair he seethes the more sharply with the desires of this world. In his mind thirst burns against him, because he who has acted perversely is inflamed to act more perversely.
18.10: 18.10 A snare is hidden in the earth. Same place. A snare is hidden in the earth when guilt is concealed under earthly advantages, so that a man sees what he may be able to desire, and yet by no means sees in what snare of guilt he sets his foot. And his trap. For the enemy observes the character of each, to which vice they are near, and sets before their face those things to which he knows the mind is more easily inclined: luxury for gentle and cheerful characters, anger and pride for harsh minds. He therefore places the trap where he sees the path of the mind to be: because he introduces the danger of deception there where he has found the way of a nearby thought.
18.11: 18.11 Fears shall terrify him on every side. Because often a person fears to be good for this reason, lest he suffer from the wicked what he remembers having done to the good: and while he fears to suffer what he does, terrified on every side, suspected on every side, he loses his step in the good work.
18.12: 18.12 Let his strength be wasted with hunger. Our flesh is weakness. But strength is the rational soul, which is able by reason to resist in fighting the vices. It is wasted with hunger when it is fed by no refreshment of inner food. And let famine invade his ribs. The ribs are the senses of the mind, which protect the hidden thoughts like the inward parts. Famine invades the ribs of the wicked man, because inner hunger weakens the senses of the mind, so that they in no way govern his thoughts within, but wander to the outward things that they seek. Let it devour the beauty of his skin and consume his arms. The same. The beauty of the skin is outward temporal glory; by the arms works are signified. He calls death sin, which kills the soul.
18.13: 18.13 The firstborn death. Pride, which is the beginning of all sin. The firstborn death therefore devours the beauty of his skin and his arms: by which pride supplants the glory or the working of the wicked. For he could have been glorious even in this life, if he had not been proud.
18.14: 18.14 Let his confidence be torn away from his tent. The same. His confidence is torn from his tent when the perverse man, who had prepared many things in this life, is scattered by sudden death. And let destruction tread upon him like a king. Because here he is either oppressed by vices that drag to destruction, or at the time of death is subjected to demonic power.
18.15: 18.15 Let them dwell in his tent. That is, let the apostate angels dwell in his mind through the most wicked thoughts, his companions, that is, who for this reason no longer is, because he has withdrawn from the supreme being. Let it be sprinkled in his tent. Same place. Sulphur is sprinkled in the tent of the wicked as often as the delight of the flesh rules in his mind. For by sulphur the stench of the flesh is understood. And because such a man remains in evil, so that he cannot even produce the fruit of good, he adds:
18.16: 18.16 Let his roots be dried up below. By roots we understand thoughts, etc., down to because all his working is reckoned as nothing by the judgment from above.
18.17: 18.17 Let his memory perish. Same place. The wicked man tries to establish his memory on earth when he strives to extend the glory of his praise. And he rejoices that his name is celebrated in the streets when he spreads the working of his iniquity far and wide. GREGORY. The head of the wicked is the devil: for he in the last times will enter that vessel of perdition which will be called Antichrist, who will try to spread his name far and wide.
18.18: 18.18 He shall drive him out from the light. He is led from light to darkness when he is condemned from the honor of the present life to eternal torments. He speaks thus of each wicked man, so that it turns to the head, that is the devil, who will extend his name in Antichrist, which the wicked now imitate. And he shall remove him from the world, etc. When, with the judge appearing from above, he is transferred from this world to punishments; all of which can also be understood of Antichrist, the head of the wicked.
18.19: 18.19 He shall have no offspring, etc. Because all the wicked, who were born by his persuasion in wicked actions, will be struck down with their same head. Because these things are to be understood of Antichrist, he reveals this when he says:
18.20: 18.20 They shall be astonished at his day. Because he will then display such great signs, etc., down to they fear the torments which they overcome. And horror shall seize the first, that is, the hearts of the elect will be struck with fear; hence it is written: So as to lead into error, if possible, even the elect (Matthew 24), not indeed to fall, but to tremble in the flesh.
18.21: 18.21 These then are the tents. He referred to this what he had said, etc., down to because they believed that holy Job was struck for iniquity.
19.2: 19.2 How long do you afflict, etc. GREGORY. The good are worn down by the words of the wicked when those who lie either in perverse faith or in wicked morals swell against them in words.
19.3: 19.3 Behold, ten times you confound me. The same. Because he had heard rebukes from them five times, and had answered five times, he declares that he has been confounded ten times. Because he endured confusion both in being gravely rebuked and in speaking words of doctrine to those who do not listen: in his own rebukes, because he makes no progress in them; in their rebukes, because he grieves at the perversity which he hears. Behold, ten times. The same. The Church keeps the Decalogue, to which the wicked cause confusion as often as they oppose the divine words in their deeds. And you are not ashamed to oppress me. There are some whom malice suddenly arising invites to commit wickedness, but yet human shame calls them back.
19.4: 19.4 Indeed, even if I was ignorant. The knowledge of heretics is not with them but against them, while it puffs up. But the ignorance of the Church, in that it cannot penetrate hidden things, is with it, because it is for it, while it humbles itself; and because what heretics seek to know is elation, so that they may seem learned against the good, he adds: you, on the contrary, should rise up against yourselves, from my being struck, fearing worse things for yourselves. For the good man is first raised against himself, afterward against others.
19.5: 19.5 But you are raised up against me. That is, you leave yourselves to be reproved, and rebuke me with strict sentences. And you reprove me. Because those who had known him to be just before the scourges now judged him unjust from that very striking.
19.6: 19.6 At least now understand. This the Lord had said of him: You have moved me against him in vain, which he himself asserts of himself: that he was not afflicted by the Lord with an equal judgment. For if his life and the scourges are weighed, he seems afflicted with an unequal judgment: but because he heaped up his merits from the scourges, God did not afflict Job with an unjust judgment. Because God not with an equal judgment. It must therefore be maintained that God both dealt rightly with Job, and yet he does not lie who says that it was not done equally: otherwise the devil would have prevailed in what he had promised about the fault of the blessed man whom God praised. This pain, not elation, wrung from him. If a good man in a humble mind, when the cause or grief demands, says good things of himself, he does not sin. And has encompassed me with his scourges. When so great an affliction presses us down that the mind cannot breathe with the consolation of anything, we are no longer merely borne along by scourges, but also encompassed, because we are surrounded on every side by the lash of tribulations.
19.7: 19.7 Behold, I shall cry out suffering violence. The same. God, knowing what will profit us, etc., down to who cannot discern even what is to be done.
19.8: 19.8 He has hedged in my path, etc. He saw his path hedged in with blows when, desiring to pass over to security, he could not escape the scourges: and, as if on the path of the heart, he found darkness of ignorance, since he could not penetrate why he was scourged in this way.
19.9: 19.9 He has stripped me of my glory. These things plainly apply to Job, etc., down to by whose falling the army falls more widely.
19.10: 19.10 He has destroyed me on every side and I perish, and as a tree torn up, etc. A tree is driven by the wind so that it falls: so the weak man is drawn by threats to injustice, and abandons the eternal things he hoped for; and because sometimes he who, terrified by punishments, abandons justice, nevertheless does not escape the punishments.
16.20: 16.20 For behold in, etc. The witness of the Son is the Father, as in the Gospel: And the Father who sent me, he has himself borne witness of me. And my conscious. Because with one will, etc., down to but he ought not to fear such rebukes of men, hence it is added.
16.21: 16.21 My friends are full of words. When friends are full of words, that is, when even those who are allied in faith detract, the eye must needs drop tears to God, that our whole intention may flow away in compunction of inmost love, and the more raise itself to inward things as by outward reproaches it is forced to return within.
16.22: 16.22 And would that, etc. We indeed are sinners, etc., down to but yet he consoles himself about its brevity.
16.23: 16.23 For behold short years pass. Everything that passes is short, and we walk in the path of death by which we do not return, not that we are not brought back to life by rising again; but because we do not come again to the labors of this mortal life, or to acquire by labors rewards.
17.1: 17.1 My spirit shall be wasted. GREGORY. The spirit of the elect is wasted by fear of the judge, and any carnal thoughts they find in themselves they consume by the ardor of penance. But the spirit of the wicked grows gross by the swelling of pride. And only the grave remains for me. He considers himself almost dead, because he is by no means ignorant that he will die, hence it follows:
17.2: 17.2 I have not sinned. He did not sin so far as to deserve these scourges, because he was struck not to correct a fault but to increase grace. Or, the head says this, who without guilt took up the punishment of guilt, that is, the bitterness of the passion.
17.3: 17.3 Set me beside you. By ascension; afterward, because Judea was moved against the disciples, he adds: Any man's hand. Because they now act in vain against him who sits in heaven.
17.4: 17.4 Their heart far. For if they knew the keeping of discipline, they would in no way despise the precepts of the Redeemer. Therefore not, etc. For those who by discipline strive not to keep their life, always through desires lie in the lowest things, and do not raise their mind to the hope of the heavenly country.
17.5: 17.5 He promises prey, etc. He turns the sentence to the head of evils, the devil, whose companions are the apostate angels, who fell with him. The sons are perverse men, who are begotten of his wicked persuasion in the working of malice. Prey therefore he promises to his companions, because he promises the souls of the wicked to the malignant spirits to be snatched at the end. The eyes of his children shall fail. Ibid. Because the intentions of men, etc., down to what they grieve they suffer without end.
17.6: 17.6 He has set me. Everyone who is struck with a scourge, etc., down to and that penalty he wishes upon his adversary which he sees befallen the just.
17.7: 17.7 My eye is dimmed with indignation. The eye grows dim with indignation when those in the Church who have the light of truth see the perverse prevail against the innocent: because they are troubled with wonder at the hidden judgment. But when the just grow dim with indignation, the weak for the most part fall even to unbelief, hence it follows: And my members as it were to nothing. By the name of members the tenderness of the weak is expressed, who, while they see the perverse flourish and the just tormented, repent of having begun good, and so withdraw the sooner to doing evil, as if the good they began had harmed their life.
17.8: 17.8 The just shall be astonished at this. This is what he had said, my eye is dimmed with indignation. And the innocent shall be raised up against the hypocrite. The perfect innocent is raised up against the hypocrite when he despises him with his flower and, preaching what is right, announces that he is to be despised by the rest.
17.9: 17.9 And the just shall hold on his way. Because, considering the hypocrite, while he sees him obtain by perverse will the things of the world, he himself is bound more strongly to the love of heavenly things. Knowing that eternal rewards will not be wanting to good desires: while temporal goods are not denied even to wicked and double hearts. And to the clean of hands shall add strength. Because seeing the earthly glory of the perverse, etc., down to which cannot be common to him with the reprobate.
17.10: 17.10 Therefore all of you. After bringing in the outward advances of the wicked, but the inward of the good, he exhorts the elect to be converted, by leaving evils, and to come, by doing good.
17.11: 17.11 And there is not among you. Desiring their conversion he wishes that he find no wise man among them, as if to say: Learn to be fools among you, that you may be truly wise in God. My days are passed. Days, prosperities: Thoughts tormenting the heart, he says, the care of earthly felicity: which the more heavily they press the elect, the more subtly they consider that account is demanded of them by the judge; these thoughts are scattered with the earthly felicity itself.
17.12: 17.12 They have turned night into day. Scattered thoughts turn night into day, because sometimes it pleases the just more to suffer evils from adversity than to be wearied by the care of earthly dispensation from prosperity. And again after darkness. Ibid. Light is hoped for after darkness, etc., down to and set the souls of the just now in a perpetual seat.
17.13: 17.13 If I wait. The earlier saints could bear adversities, etc., down to had prepared rest for themselves in hell.
17.14: 17.14 I have said to rottenness. He calls rottenness father, etc., down to that as by worms we are wearied in mind by restless thoughts.
17.15: 17.15 Where is now then my expectation. The expectation of the just is Christ; whom they knew would come at some time, but sought that he come sooner: hence here is added, now: And my patience who considers? God considers the patience of the just; but he is said as it were not to consider, to appear less quickly to the wish of desire: and to defer the grace of his dispensation to longer times.
17.16: 17.16 All that is mine shall go down into the deepest pit. Before the coming of the mediator Job was to go down into hell, etc., down to the reward was still awaited to be received only in the rest of hell. Do you think there will be at least rest for me? It is to be weighed which of us can be secure of rest: if even he trembles for it, the heralds of whose virtue even the judge who strikes proclaims.
18.2: 18.2 How long will you throw out words? GREGORY, on Job, book 14. He alleges that blessed Job has broken out into pride, whom he declares to throw out words. Understand first. It signals with how great elation he had swelled, who thought Job to speak what he did not understand.
18.3: 18.3 Why are we counted. It is proper to the human mind to suspect that to be done to itself which it does. For he who is accustomed to despise the good thinks himself despised: and from the suspicion of contempt he leaps to indignation and heaps up insults.
18.4: 18.4 Why do you destroy your soul. The reprobate esteem the zeal of rectitude, or the spiritual grace of holy preaching, the madness of fury: by which they think the souls of the faithful perish. Shall the earth be forsaken for you. The Church says, etc., down to hence this man insults the scourges of Job, whence he adds:
18.5: 18.5 Shall not the light of the wicked be extinguished. This could rightly be said of the wicked, against the holy it should not: Light he calls the prosperity of the present life. But the light of the wicked is extinguished, because the prosperity of the fleeting life ends when it ends. Neither shall the flame of his fire shine. Fire he calls the fervor of temporal desires, whose flame is the beauty or outward power which proceeds from his inner ardor: but it shall not shine, because on the day of departure all outward beauty is taken away.
18.6: 18.6 The light shall be dark in his tabernacle. Sometimes we take sadness as darkness, joy as light. The light then grows dark in the tabernacle of the wicked, because in his conscience the joy which had come from temporal things fails. And the lamp that is over him shall be put out. A lamp is a light in a pot, etc., down to because earthly joys possess the mind of the wicked.
18.7: 18.7 The steps of his strength shall be straitened, etc. Because the strength of his malice, which he now exercises, punishment will afterward constrain. And shall cast him down. The wicked man now has the counsel to desire present things, etc., down to which he expresses when he adds.
18.8: 18.8 For he has thrust his feet into a net. Ibid. He who thrusts his feet into a net does not cast them out when he will. So he who casts himself into sins does not rise at once when he will. And walks in its meshes. Ibid. He who walks in the meshes of a net entangles his steps by walking: and when he strives to extricate himself for walking, he is bound that he may not walk.
19.11: 19.11 His wrath is kindled against me. For he who is struck so that his strength is overcome, God does not strike him as a son by discipline but as an enemy by wrath: hence the prophet: I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with a cruel chastisement, Jeremiah 30. And because often the malignant spirits persuade the hearts of the afflicted to many things, and steal any good there is, he adds:
19.12: 19.12 His robbers came together. That is the malignant spirits, who are busy in searching out the morals of men: who make a way for themselves in the hearts of the afflicted, when amid the adversities which are outwardly borne they do not cease to send in wicked thoughts too. And they besieged round about my tabernacle, etc. They besiege the tabernacle round about, etc., down to they have worn out all his body with ulcers.
19.13: 19.13 My brethren far from me. Ibid. Now he uses the voice of the Redeemer: far from him are made his brethren, and his acquaintance withdrew; those who, holding the law, knew how to prophesy of him, and did not recognize him present. For the Jews, near by flesh and known by the instruction of the law, as if forgetting him of whom by faith they had prophesied in the words of the law, denied him incarnate in words of perfidy.
19.15: 19.15 The sojourners of my house. That is the priests, whose origin was deputed to the service of God, but by office they were already held in the condition of a handmaid. The souls of the Levites are in the secrets of the tabernacle, as in the inner parts of the chamber serving more familiarly. And I was like a stranger, etc. Because by the synagogue he was not known; hence the prophet also: You shall be as a husbandman in the land, and as a wayfaring man turning aside to lodge, Jeremiah 14. For he who was not heard as Lord was believed not a possessor of the field but a husbandman: Who as a wayfarer turned aside to abide, because he took few from Judea, and, going on to the calling of the Gentiles, completed the journey begun.
19.16: 19.16 I called my servant. The servant was the Jewish people, obedient from fear; whom, by bestowing gifts, as if by voices sent out, he determined to bring to himself, but he did not answer, because he scorned to render worthy works to his gifts. I entreated him with my own mouth. I who had commanded him so many precepts by the mouth of the prophets, entreated with my own mouth: because shown in the flesh, while he humbly spoke the commands of life, he as it were asked the proud servant to come.
19.17: 19.17 My wife abhorred my breath, etc. The wife of the Lord, etc., down to who, given to carnal senses, did not recognize the mystery of his incarnation. And I entreated the children of my womb. The womb of God we ought to take as his counsel; in which before the ages by predestination we were conceived, that created we might be brought forth through the ages. He therefore entreated the children of his womb: because those whom he made, incarnate he humbly entreated.
19.18: 19.18 Even fools despised me, etc. Because while the lawyers despised God, the crowd of the people followed their unbelief. The wise being left, he had come to seek the poor and the foolish: hence with increase of sorrow he says Even fools; for whom I took up folly, the Word made flesh, they despised me. And when I departed from them. As it were the Lord approached to the heart of the peoples when he showed them miracles: and as it were withdrew when he showed no signs, and they would not give faith to one resting from miracles.
19.19: 19.19 They abhorred me, etc. The scribes and doctors of the law, etc., down to concerning the same order of teachers of the law it follows: And he whom I loved most. The order of teachers, which formerly serving in preaching was most loved: whom the crowd followed not only to not believe but even to persecute God. And then was done what follows:
19.20: 19.20 My bone has cleaved to my skin. In the bones is fortitude, etc., down to at the time of the passion found beside him women. The flesh. GREGORY. What had clung to the bone, while the disciples, though weak, preached the faith of truth to the peoples. And when the holy women prepared the outward bodily aids that were necessary, they remained as the skin outside on the body. And left. The teeth are the apostles; the lips only were left around the teeth, when two walking after his death knew how to talk with him, but now feared to preach him or to bite the vices of the unbelievers. But now he returns to Job's own words. Only. Nor for the happy is there anything around the teeth but lips: and so it is plain this is said mystically.
19.21: 19.21 Have pity on me. It belongs to the pious, when they suffer from adversaries, to be moved not so much to anger as to prayers. He calls himself touched by the hand of the Lord, as Satan himself had said: Put forth your hand and touch his bone.
19.22: 19.22 Why do you persecute me. The more justly God strikes others' vices, the less he has of vices in himself. And the sense is: You afflict me thus for my infirmities as if you yourselves had nothing of infirmity after the manner of God. As God. They act the same as God, because they do what God omnipotent permits to be done; but they do not wish the same: because when omnipotent God shows purgation by loving, the depravity of the unjust exercises malice by raging. Or, as not infirm, who ought not to rebuke when God strikes, lest they add sorrow to sorrow, but console. But when the hand of the Lord ceases, then rebuke can be made to the worthy. And are filled with my flesh. Those whose mind hungers for the punishments of their neighbors seek to be filled with others' flesh. Or, those who feed on detraction of another's life are filled with others' flesh. Who will grant me, etc. The hard things he endures he does not wish covered by silence, but drawn to notice by example that others may be edified to patience. Who will grant me. Ibid. These things also befit the Church, etc., down to but afterwards the book itself he divides into a plate of lead and flint. Who will give me, etc. By the iron pen the strong sentence of the Fathers. By lead the people of Judea heavy with sin. By flint the Gentile world is figured. All that he bore therefore, taught by the strong sentence of the Fathers, both the people of Judea and the Gentile world knew. What is written in lead is quickly erased. On flint it is hard to engrave, but it remains: so Judea quickly received the words of God, and quickly abandoned them. The Gentile world scarcely received, but having received kept them strongly.
19.25: 19.25 For I know that my Redeemer, etc. He does not say Maker, but Redeemer, openly announcing him, who after he created all things redeemed us from captivity by his passion. He lives, however, who fell among the hands of the wicked. And in the last day I shall rise out of the earth, and again, etc. Ibid. Because the resurrection, etc., down to by which flower he is shown a priest, who intercedes for us.
19.27: 19.27 Whom I myself shall see, etc. GREGORY. Our flesh after the resurrection will be the same and different. The same by nature, different by glory. And it shall be spiritual, because incorruptible and palpable: because it will not lose the essence of true nature. I myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. He expressly indicates the truth of the resurrection: for it is not one who dies and another who rises, as those who say the body will be invisible and impalpable, as Eutychius said, but the very same. This my hope is laid up in my bosom. We believe we have nothing more certain, etc., down to hence he straightway adds:
19.28: 19.28 Why then now. The perverse, because they wish to find accusation in the tongue of the just, seek the root of the word from which they take the origin of speaking, and spread the branches of talkativeness: but yet the holy man, pitying, shows the evils they should flee.
19.29: 19.29 Flee therefore. Ibid. To flee the face of the sword is to appease the sentence of strict punishment before it appears. And know that there is a judgment. Everyone who acts perversely, by that very fact that he despises this, does not know there is a judgment of God.
20.1: 20.1 Therefore my thoughts. GREGORY on Job, book 15. As if to say: because I consider the terror of the last judgment, therefore I am confounded in fear by tumults of thoughts. And the mind is snatched in different directions. When now the evils he neglected to do, now the blameworthy things in which he is, now the right things which he sees are still wanting to him, he weighs with anxious fear. These of the company of Job knew indeed how to live rightly, but not knowing how to weigh subtly the judgments of God, they believe the just cannot be struck here. And therefore they suspected him unjust, and slide into rebuke: to which, however, they descend with a certain reverence. Hence this one adds.
20.3: 20.3 The doctrine by which, etc. Ibid. These things being moderately premised, etc., down to and this I find, that the praise of the wicked, etc.
20.4: 20.4 This I know from the beginning. For if from the very rise of the human race to this time we lead the eyes of the mind, everything that could be ended we see how short it was.
20.5: 20.5 And the joy of the hypocrite. The joy of the hypocrite is like a point. For as a pen on a point, while it is placed, is lifted, so the hypocrite, while he touches the praise of the present life, loses it. Like a point, because the gladness passes, the punishment remains: it appears for a moment, disappears forever.
20.6: 20.6 If he ascend, that is, even if he pretends to live a heavenly life, even if he displays an understanding like true preachers, yet like a dunghill at last he shall perish, because his mind will be condemned for the stench of its vices.
20.7: 20.7 And they that had seen him shall say. Ibid. Those who saw him elated, he being extinguished, will say, Where is he? because neither in this world where he had been elated does he appear, nor in the rest of eternity, to which he was thought to belong.
20.8: 20.8 As a dream that flies away. The life of the hypocrite, etc., down to because sleeping he saw the favors of men.
20.9: 20.9 The eye that had seen him. The place of the hypocrite is the heart of flatterers: for there he rests where he finds favors. The eye therefore that had seen him shall not see, because in death he is hidden from his lovers who were accustomed to behold him with admiration. Neither shall he any more behold. Because the tongues of the flatterers do not follow him to judgment with favors.
20.10: 20.10 His children shall be crushed, etc. Because those who are born in hypocrisy from imitation of him, while they hold not the solidity of truth, fail in poverty of heart.
20.11: 20.11 His bones shall be filled. The youth of the hypocrite is the beginning of wickedness, etc., down to to be emptied of all solidity and perish.
20.12: 20.12 For when it was sweet. Ibid. In the mouth of the heart iniquity is sweet, which he covers under the cloak of bland speech. For the evil would be on the tongue, and not under the tongue, if the hypocrite in speaking revealed the malice. He will spare it and not. He spares the evil he loves who does not pursue it by repenting; and does not forsake it, but hides it in the throat, because he so keeps it in thought that he never brings it out in voice. BEDE. That is, he fondles, cherishes and nourishes his evil, and delighting in it never repents so as to depart from it.
20.14: 20.14 His bread in his belly. Often the hypocrite strives to be instructed by the bread of sacred speech, not to live by it, but to appear learned; but while he wrongly understands the word of doctrine which he seeks ill, and falls into heresies: it happens to him that as from the gall of asps, so he dies from the bread. But because the words of God, even if he understands rightly, he in no way keeps in work, he loses them in the present life so that he does not know what he wished to do.
20.15: 20.15 Riches. Of the sacred law which by reading he devoured, he will vomit by forgetting: which God by just judgment plucks from his memory. The head of asps. Ibid. The asp is a little serpent, etc., down to as the viper kills by its tongue.
20.17: 20.17 Let him not see the rivulets. Ibid. The rivulets of the river are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, etc., down to signifies the mystery of the incarnation of Christ.
20.18: 20.18 He shall pay for all he did. For he shall pay in torment for the desires which he here kept unlawful, and he shall not be consumed in death, but that he may be tortured without end, he is compelled to live without end, that he whose life here was dead in guilt, there his death may live in punishment. Let him say then, he shall pay for all he did, and yet shall not be consumed, because he is tortured and not extinguished: he dies and lives, fails and always subsists, and is without end.
20.19: 20.19 Because he broke in pieces. He breaks in pieces and strips the house of the poor, because him whom by power he crushes he is not ashamed to despoil by avarice.
20.20: 20.20 Nor was his belly filled. The belly of the unjust is avarice, and in it is gathered whatever is swallowed by perverse desire. It is manifest that avarice is not extinguished by the things desired but increased; for like fire, when it has received wood to consume, it grows, and whence the flame seems for a moment to be pressed, thence a little after it is seen to spread. And when he has what he desired. It is of greater wrath when what is wickedly desired is granted, because sudden vengeance follows, since he also obtained what he coveted God being angry.
20.21: 20.21 Nothing remained of his city. The hypocrite being struck, nothing of his food remains, because when he is led to punishments he is alienated from all he possessed. Therefore nothing, etc. Because, taken from this life, he goes naked to the judge.
20.22: 20.22 When he shall be filled, he shall be straitened. GREGORY. When he has heaped up much he is straitened; for he is anxious how to keep what he has acquired. He shall be in a heat, and every sorrow. On this side and that he fears plotters, etc., down to the more easily is he dragged to torment. It follows:
20.23: 20.23 Would that his belly were filled, etc., let God rain war upon him. For God to rain war, etc., down to he scorned to foresee.
20.24: 20.24 He shall flee from arms. Ibid. The covetous man sometimes steals others' things, etc., down to he sets himself before the strokes of eternal judgment. Meanwhile,
20.25: 20.25 The sword drawn, etc. The wicked man, while he plots wicked things in thought, is as a sword in the sheath. It comes out of the sheath while by iniquity it is opened to evil working; drawn out by the seducer, but coming out by his own will, They shall go and come, etc. The malignant spirits are to good minds, etc., down to elation is substituted for continence, etc.
20.26: 20.26 All darkness is hid. For he who does not fulfill all things at once in effect holds in silence in mind all that may harm. A fire shall devour him, etc. The fire of Gehenna which is not kindled by human effort but was created by God from the beginning of the world. He that is left shall be afflicted. The tabernacle of the wicked is the flesh, because he gladly dwells in it, with which his spirit will be tormented. The good place not their joy in the flesh but in heaven. Left by the flesh from which he is drawn away, which he loved here and would not leave: then because of the torments he will wish to leave it, but will not be able.
20.27: 20.27 The heaven shall reveal; Ibid. because he here spared neither good nor bad, in the dread examination the life of the just and of sinners will alike accuse him.
20.28: 20.28 It shall be open. When every evil which was born in his conscience is shown at the coming of the judge. He shall be drawn in: because at the time of vengeance, snatched to punishments, he is separated from the face of the eternal judge.
20.29: 20.29 This is the portion of the wicked man. For when the justice of God exacts punishment from the reprobate for their perverse acts, it renders them evils even to the retribution of words.
21.4: 21.4 Is my dispute against man? Blessed Job, if pleasing God he displeased men, would have no causes of sadness; but because he believed he had displeased God by the present scourges, made doubtful about his past life, he now called his mind to sadness: who if with the scourges absent he disputed against man about the merits of his life, ought by no means to have been saddened. Is my dispute against man. As if not yet a hypocrite, if I dealt with men about my life I would not fear: if I displeased them I would not care; but because with God, rightly I am sad. But you attend to me, as God, yet I fear you not.
21.5: 21.5 Attend, that is consider what I have done, and wonder at what I suffer. And lay your finger on your mouth, that is join to your speech the virtue of discretion.
21.6: 21.6 And when I remember. Ibid. Because he was not forgetful of his deeds, etc., down to against his sayings he adds:
21.7: 21.7 Why then do the wicked live. They are lifted up with honors, strengthened with riches, because divine patience bears with them. Strengthened with riches, etc., that they may be allowed to stand long in them; but because there are those for whom to have these things is punishment, because they have no heirs to whom to leave them. He adds:
21.8: 21.8 Their seed continues. To the increase of felicity heirs are given with the patrimony. Before them. Lest any necessity take away even from their eyes the things in which the mind exults; but lest the race be extinguished in these barren, he adds: A crowd of kinsmen and grandchildren in their sight. Behold life, honors, riches, sons, grandchildren are said to be theirs: but if within domestic care burned, this felicity would not be glad, hence he adds:
21.9: 21.9 Their houses are secure, and peaceful, and not. For what would the aforesaid felicity be if it were not glad? If prosperous within, in the fields too. Their ox has conceived. To lords of flocks the first felicity is, etc., down to hence the fruitfulness of the household is added:
21.11: 21.11 They go out like flocks. That as greater things are granted to be had, so many may sprout up to guard them. And their children exult in sports. But lest we believe that sport vile, he says:
21.12: 21.12 They take the timbrel and harp. As if when the lords swell with honors and riches, the subjects rejoice in sportive acts.
21.13: 21.13 They spend their days in good. Because the whole length of the present life is known to be a point, when it ends in an end. For whatever could pass was sudden. And in a point they go down to hell. But the end is the worst; behold where it was tending, because the prosperity of the present life is not a witness of innocence, because both those who use it perish and the scourged are freed, which is against Job's friends.
21.14: 21.14 Who said to God: Depart from us. GREGORY. They say to God: Depart from us, who refuse him access to themselves, and fight him by wicked acts. The knowledge of your ways. The way of God is peace, humility, patience: which those who despise say: We desire not the knowledge of your ways.
21.15: 21.15 Who is the Almighty? etc. For the fool has said in his heart: There is no God. And what does it profit us if we pray to him? The wicked, who seek not God but outward gifts, when they see the same lacking to the raging, themselves scorn to serve.
21.16: 21.16 Yet because they are not. He has goods in his hand who, despising temporal things, keeps them under the dominion of the mind. But whoever loves them too much subjects himself to them more than they to himself. The counsel of the wicked far. The counsel of the wicked is to seek earthly glory, to neglect the eternal. But because in this life they are not continually prosperous, it follows:
21.17: 21.17 How often shall the lamp of the wicked be put out. Often the wicked man reckons the life of his sons his lamp; but when a son who is too much loved is taken away, the lamp of the wicked, which seemed, is extinguished; so it is with riches and honors. And a flood shall come upon them. A flood comes upon the wicked when they suffer waves of sorrows from some adversity. And he shall divide sorrows, etc. He who keeps eternal sorrows for the wicked man, and here sometimes pierces his mind with temporal sorrow; because he strikes here and there, he divides the sorrows of his fury upon the wicked, that he may be crushed by a double contrition.
21.18: 21.18 They shall be as chaff. Because by the blast of the wrath of God they are suddenly lifted and carried to the fire: And as the dust which, because the whirlwind snatching them carries them off to eternal punishments.
21.19: 21.19 God shall lay up for his children. Because he who imitates the iniquity of a parent is bound also by his fault. And when he shall have rendered. For the wicked man knows not the evils he has done until he begins to be punished.
21.20: 21.20 His eyes shall see. Because he had so hardened in iniquity that he did not fear to have struck even in them the things he loved, provided he fulfilled what he had perversely planned: of which hardening it is added:
21.21: 21.21 For what to. Not that in hell he thinks not of his kinsmen, etc., down to lest anyone presume to examine, it follows:
21.22: 21.22 Shall any teach God knowledge? that is, he deals nothing unjustly with us, who justly judged even the angelic nature, subtler than ours, hence nothing remains to complain of.
21.23: 21.23 One dies. Behold he puts those things in which anyone might examine the secret of the Almighty by asking why he permits these things so to be. The surface of the letter is plain enough of itself. What he says:
21.24: 21.24 His bowels are full of fat. Fat is from abundant food, etc., down to behold the rich man rejoices in vain, the poor is afflicted more vainly.
21.26: 21.26 And yet they shall sleep together in the dust. Ibid. What care for the unlike life, prosperous or adverse, when the end is alike in dust? That life is to be thought of where with the resurrection one comes to an unlike end, where the happy goes to punishments, the afflicted passes to rest. And yet together in the dust. That is, in earthly desires they shall close the eyes of the mind: And worms, which come from flesh, that is carnal cares press, which was not in Job, who neither swelled with what he had nor was anxious over what he lost. But they think this, therefore he adds:
21.27: 21.27 Surely I know your thoughts. For whom they saw struck, etc., down to nor perfectly pass to eternal things, hence he adds:
21.29: 21.29 Ask any one of the way. A traveler is called one who considers the present life a way to himself and not the homeland, who scorns to fix his heart on the love of the passing age, but seeks the eternal.
21.31: 21.31 Who shall reprove before him his way. When he spoke of the body of all the wicked, etc., down to neither Elijah nor Enoch by their own strength, but God's.
21.32: 21.32 He shall be brought to the graves. This in life, etc., down to because he will be received only in the hearts of the wicked. And in the heap. Because in the congregation of sinners he displays the snares of his craftiness; and since the wicked are many, they are rightly called a heap.
21.33: 21.33 He was sweet. Cocytus is called the mourning of the weak, etc., down to signifying that there is unjust mourning. And after him every. Ibid. The man wise in human wisdom is here understood; he draws after him every man, because he snatches all whom he finds carnal under the yoke of his dominion: who even now, before he appears, draws innumerable ones, though not all, because many are drawn back from carnality.
21.34: 21.34 How then do you comfort, etc. Since, if the wicked in this life is permitted to prosper, which was shown of Antichrist, it is necessary that the elect be held under the bridle of the scourge. When your answer, etc. For they could not comfort him in whom by their words they opposed the truth. For when they called him hypocrite, because by lying they committed a fault, they increased the punishment of the afflicted just; because the fault of another's falsehood tortures him who loves the truth.
22.1: 22.1 Answering, etc. Can man be compared to God? GREGORY, on Job, book 16. Those who fail against the words of truth repeat even known things, lest by silence they seem conquered; hence Eliphaz, pressed by the speeches of blessed Job, says what no one is ignorant of; for he says: Can man be compared to God? For in comparison with God, knowledge, etc., down to as if descending he adds.
22.3: 22.3 What does it profit? In everything that we do well, etc., down to Eliphaz adds yet what no one is ignorant of.
22.4: 22.4 Shall he fearing reprove you? Who, even if foolish, would think that God reproves us from fear, and from dread proposes his judgment against us? Shall he reprove you? Those who know not how to measure their words slip into idle speeches.
22.5: 22.5 And not for your great malice. From idle words, etc., down to but always descends to worse. For it follows.
22.6: 22.6 For you have taken away a pledge. These things are plain according to the letter, etc., down to or lose spiritual gifts, who come to you.
22.9: 22.9 Widows. The heretics say the peoples, etc., down to they say is repaid for sins? And this is, Therefore you are surrounded with snares.
22.11: 22.11 And you thought. As if he said, etc., down to as wave upon wave.
22.12: 22.12 Do you not think that God. As if, or therefore, etc., down to because by foolish judgment they think themselves alone wise.
22.15: 22.15 Do you desire to keep the path? As the path of the Redeemer is humility, so the path of the ages is pride. The path of the ages therefore the wicked men tread, who through the desires of this life walk about in elation.
22.16: 22.16 Who were taken away before their time; except that all. Those who love the present life, etc., down to and the sentence is changed, but not the eternal counsel. And a river overthrew their foundation. The wicked, while they do not see present things to be fleeting, etc., down to because the course of mutability undermines in them the state of the perverse construction.
22.18: 22.18 Whereas he had filled. The Lord fills the houses of the wicked, because even to the ungrateful he does not deny his gifts. Whose counsel far. This Job also, etc., down to he wishes to be unlike the wicked.
22.19: 22.19 The just shall see the destruction of the wicked. And shall rejoice. When they have adhered to the strict judge with now perfect security. For now they look on the reprobate and groan.
22.20: 22.20 Is not cut down. Here the wicked are lifted up, etc., down to or are dragged from the sight of the judge to Gehenna. And fire has devoured their remnants. Because even if here they leave the flesh, in the resurrection they will receive it, to burn in the flesh in which they sinned.
22.21: 22.21 Submit therefore. It is a fault of pride to teach a better man, which heretics often do to Catholics.
22.23: 22.23 If you return. Because you were destroyed from the building of justice. And far the face. The body is taken as the tabernacle of the soul and the mind as that of thoughts. And the sense is: If you return to God after errors, you shall be cleansed in thought and in work.
22.24: 22.24 He shall give for earth. By earth the weakness of action is signified, by flint fortitude, by golden torrents the doctrine of inmost clarity. To those converted to himself he gives for earth the flint of robust work, and for flint golden torrents. For. Because for robust work he multiplies the doctrine of clear preaching. BEDE. He says this, that if the Lord is propitiated, etc., down to are silver tried by fire.
22.25: 22.25 And the Almighty shall be against. Ibid. Often when we attend to sacred speech we heavily bear the snares of malignant spirits. And the sense is: when he has driven the malignant spirits from you, the bright talent of divine speech shall grow in you.
22.26: 22.26 Then upon. To abound in delights upon the Almighty is to be satisfied in love of him with the feasts of sacred Scripture. And you shall lift up to God. To lift the face to God is to raise the heart to search out sublime things.
22.27: 22.27 And you shall pay your vows. He who has vowed vows but cannot pay for weakness, for him it is done by the punishment of sin that the power for good be withdrawn from the willing: but when the fault that stands in the way is wiped away, it follows at once that the possibility follows the vow.
22.28: 22.28 You shall decree. A thing is decreed and comes, when virtue, which is sought from desire, by the Lord's bestowal prospers even in effect. And it shall come. The same the heretics promise to the afflicted, if they follow them. And in your ways. In the ways of the just to shine with light is to sprinkle the signs of their brightness by wonderful works of virtue.
22.29: 22.29 For he that has been humbled. Because he who humbles himself shall be exalted. And he who. As far as can be detected by the ministry of the members, the first display of pride is wont to be in the eyes.
22.30: 22.30 The innocent shall be saved. Because when grace comes here that he become innocent, when he is led to judgment, he is rewarded by merit.
23.1: 23.1 And Job answering said: Even now in bitterness. GREGORY. The mind of the just is always in bitterness, etc., down to who by sweet speeches seek to seduce.
23.2: 23.2 And the hand of my wound. The hand of the wound is the strength of the stroke, but because from adversities the just thirst more for the face of the author, it follows:
23.3: 23.3 Who will grant me. The elect, when they see anything done contrary to their wish, run back to the hidden judgments of God, that in them they may see that what seems to run disorderly outside is not disorderly disposed within. And this is what he adds: I would find him. As it is: that God now delays that he may be the more desired. And I would come even to his seat. The seat are the angels, etc., down to while they see God disposing better things, hence: I would set judgment before God. To set judgment before God, etc., down to to consider how terrible the judge, now hidden and silent, will afterward appear.
23.4: 23.4 I would fill my mouth. Because while he contemplates the examination of the judge against himself, he pursues himself with the invective of bitter penance.
23.5: 23.5 That I may know the words, etc. For when we pursue our faults by penance we find what the judge could say of them in his examination, which he does not know, because he neglects his evils.
23.6: 23.6 I would not that he contend with great strength. For who can be found just in the examination, if God should examine the life of men according to the majesty of his strength: for however just a man, if strictly judged, he is pressed by the mass of the greatness, hence he adds: Nor with greatness. As if he said: If he contended with me according to his strength, he would press me with his bulk. And note, that while he shuns strength he longs for the infirmity of the incarnation, hence he adds:
23.7: 23.7 Let him propose equity. The Mediator of God and men, etc., down to I as victor shall exclude the judgment of my absolution.
23.8: 23.8 If I go to the east. Ibid. As if he said: The incarnate Son, etc., down to But not even in all these does the soul fully know itself, hence:
23.10: 23.10 But he knows the way. That is, I cannot see him seeing me. And he has tried. Not elated he compares himself to gold, but considers his own things humbly, which is lawful for every just man. And this is: And prove me as gold. For by the burning of tribulation both vices are taken away and merits increased.
23.11: 23.11 My foot has followed his steps. Blessed Job in future operation, etc., down to he runs back as to an example set before him.
23.12: 23.12 And in my bosom I have hid. In the bosom of the heart we hide the words of his mouth, because we hear his commands not for passing, but to be fulfilled in work, and though the words come forth in work, yet they lie hid in the heart. If within the mind is not lifted up, but praise is sought outside, then the word of God is not hid in the bosom.
23.13: 23.13 For he alone is. Principally and unchangeably. For he alone is of himself, who does all things, in which he himself is to be feared, not what we suffer. Of whose unchangeableness he adds: And no one can turn aside. Because judgments once fixed can by no means be changed. And his soul. That very force by which he disposes all things is called his soul.
23.14: 23.14 When he has fulfilled. He fulfills his will in me, because he afflicts me with many strokes. But many like things are ready to hand with him, because if he thinks to strike, there is yet found where the wound may grow.
23.15: 23.15 And therefore from his face. He is shaken by the dread of rectitude when he sees himself not fit to give an account if strictly judged.
23.16: 23.16 God has softened. The power of his strength he therefore ascribes not to himself but to the author. He has troubled me. The hearts of the just are never secure, but troubled with fear of the judge, which yet are comforted by the gifts they have received, hence: For I have not perished. The scourges of the just either purge past sins or avert future ones, which in Job's case, not in him, increases virtue.
23.17: 23.17 For not. He placed under the scourge perishes from bodily health on account of the impending darkness, who is struck for the past, to be hidden from future punishments.
24.1: 24.1 But. Because even if we now know God by faith, we see not how his eternity is without past or future. Blessed Job, lest he be wise beyond what is meet to be wise, testifying that the days of the Lord cannot be comprehended, soon turns his mind's regard to the pride of heretics: who seek to be wise in high things, of whom it follows:
24.2: 24.2 Some have removed the landmarks. Whom, under the name of others, etc., down to and nourish by pestiferous doctrines for slaughter.
24.3: 24.3 They have driven away the ass of the fatherless. He calls the elect the fatherless, etc., down to they repel from the ministry of the good. And they have taken away. The Church is called a widow, etc., down to that they may draw their followers too, hence he adds:
24.4: 24.4 They have overthrown the poor. Sometimes those who seem meek and humble, if they know not how to keep discretion, fall by the examples of others.
24.5: 24.5 Others like wild asses. For there are heretics who shun mixing with the peoples, but seek the retreat of a more secret life, and infect with the plague of their persuasion the more, as they seem the more reverend as it were from the merits of their life. They are compared to wild asses who, let loose in their pleasures from the bond of faith, are alien to reason. They go forth. For they do their own work not God's, while they follow not right dogmas but their own desires. And watching for prey. They watch for prey who always strive to seize the words of the just for their own sense, that by this they may prepare for their perverse sons the bread of error.
24.6: 24.6 A field not their own. By the name of field or vineyard the Church is signified, which perverse preachers reap, and gather the vintage, oppressing its Author in his members: who, pursuing the grace of the Creator, while they seize some from it who seemed upright, what else do they but take away the ears or grapes of souls?
24.7: 24.7 They send men away naked. As garments protect the body, so good works protect the soul. When therefore heretics destroy the good works of some, they take away the garments. To whom not. The covering belongs to justice, etc., down to they die without the garment of good work. Whom the showers of the mountains water. That is the streams of the preachers satisfy. And having not. By stones he means strong men, etc., down to they embrace stones?
24.10: 24.10 To the naked and walking without clothing. He who does neither good nor evil, etc., down to as we take away the chaff of the ears of grain, that we may be refreshed by the marrow of the spirit.
24.11: 24.11 Who tread the winepresses. GREGORY. Those who persecute the Church, etc., down to in their acts they rest as at noon.
24.12: 24.12 Out of the cities they have made men groan. Because the cities by the peoples living together, etc., down to those who run the way of God not slackly but manfully.
24.13: 24.13 And the soul of the wounded has cried out. The soul of the just is wounded when the faith of the weak is troubled; it cries out, however, while it pines at another's fall. They have been rebellious to the light. They are rebellious to the light who, following their own desires, despise the good they know. They knew not its ways. For those who first are rebellious by knowing are afterward blinded, so as not to know. Nor have they returned. The path is narrower than the way. Those who scorn to do the plainer things do not arrive at understanding the subtler; God waited, however, that they might go on by his paths; but would that they had wished to return by them, so that the journeys of life which they knew through innocence they might at least keep through penance.
24.14: 24.14 The murderer rises at first light. Because every perverse man, in the prosperity of the present life, which is designated by morning, kills by oppressing the life of the humble, and placed in adversity and dejection, which is designated by night, wounds secretly by wicked counsels like a thief.
24.15: 24.15 The eye of the adulterer. This is said of heretics: For as he who commits adultery unlawfully joins to himself the flesh of another's wife, so heretics, when they snatch the faithful soul into their error, as it were take away another's wife. And he will cover his face. The face of the human heart is the likeness of God, which the perverse man covers, that he may not be recognized by the strict judge when he confounds his life by evil acts, whence he shall say: I never knew you.
24.16: 24.16 He digs through. By the name of houses, etc., down to they scarcely dared to speak perverse things. As in. Because when they saw the just in prosperity, since they could not speak, they will give themselves to malignant counsels against them.
24.17: 24.17 If suddenly. For when they see the just break out to the height of ruling power, they are disturbed. These rejoice at the casting down of the good, but if suddenly the dawn appear, that is, if the good come to rule, they think it the shadow of death, because they fear that what they did perversely will be punished, they do not wish to be corrected, but choose to go loosely and rejoice in guilt, hence he says And so in. Because they so rejoice in the night of sin as if the light of justice shone round them; or, in present blindness they are so glad as if they already enjoyed the light of the eternal country.
24.18: 24.18 He is light upon the face of the water. The surface of the water this way and that, etc., down to hence the sentence often returns to him who is the author of evil. Cursed be his portion. Ibid. Whoever in the present life does right, etc., down to is yet held in the guilt of eternal curse. Let him not walk by the way of the vineyards. He walks by the way of the vineyards who, weighing the preacher of the universal Church, declines neither from the faith nor from the rectitude of good acts.
24.19: 24.19 He shall pass to excessive heat. Iniquity is compared to cold, etc., down to that he may believe those preaching right things he adds:
24.20: 24.20 And even to hell his sin. The sin is led even to hell which is not amended before the end of life.
24.21: 24.21 His sweetness. Because it is of the nature of worms, etc., down to the corruption and stench of rottenness is loved. Let him not be remembered. God looks upon the life of the wicked and forgets, because what he judges by strictness of sentence, as far as the memory of mercy is concerned, he is ignorant of.
24.22: 24.22 For he has fed the barren. In this place the barren is called flesh: which while it seeks present things alone, knows not to beget good thoughts: And the widows. The widow is called the soul, etc., down to it scorns to serve.
24.23: 24.23 He has pulled down the strong. In the strength of his depravity he pulls down the strong, when by the craftiness of his error he seizes the powerful of this world. And when he shall stand. The perverse preacher stands in this world as long as he lives in an earthly body, but refuses to believe in his life, because he scorns to know the truth of God. His eyes, however. GREGORY on Job, book 17. The sinner looks upon his ways, because he strives to think and see only what aids him to temporal advantage.
24.24: 24.24 They are lifted up for a little while. For they cannot subsist who are divided from eternal solidity. And shall be brought low as all. All earthly things surely. And the sense is: They cannot stand in any way, because even the things they lean on flee: and while they love temporal things they run with them and with the volubility of time. And as the tops of ears, etc. The tops of the ears are the beards, etc., down to by the strength of the last threshing it is broken, and the grains appear.
24.25: 24.25 And if it be not so, etc. Ibid. The sense is: All things are as I have set forth, etc., down to yet it is not fitting that he be judged by the wicked. Who can convict me of lying. As if to say: What I speak you cannot set before the judge, because you sinners hide his face from you. He sets deceitful words before God who examines them within himself in the sight of truth, who, considering the inner judge, weighs the outward things.
25.1: 25.1 And answering, etc. Ibid. Because Job said many things, etc., down to which he knows not when it lacks by the right of the same power?
25.2: 25.2 Who makes concord. The highest things are composed into concord, etc., down to what they cannot obtain they never wish.
25.3: 25.3 Is there any numbering? In human knowledge the number of the higher spirits is not, because how great the multitude of the invisible army there is, it knows not: who are called soldiers, because they strive against the aerial powers, not by labor but by command. And upon. Because the strength of the same soldiers, or of the elect, is strengthened not by their own forces but by the infusion of heavenly grace: which if it did not rise in our heart, surely our mind would remain in darkness, hence he adds:
25.4: 25.4 Can man be justified? Because man is born of a woman subject to guilt, the weakness of the first guilt is propagated in the offspring.
25.5: 25.5 Behold even. By the moon the Church, by the stars the souls of each one living well are designated: who perfectly desire to subdue faults. But as long as they are bound by the corruption of the flesh, bound by its chains, how much more is man rottenness!
25.6: 25.6 And the son, as if to say, etc., down to as from man the son of man, so from rottenness the worm is born.
26.1: 26.1 And Job answering. The words of the friends finished, now at the last Job rises more sharply against them, as is the custom of the skilled, to keep the stronger things for the conclusion. Ibid. Whose helper art you? Is it the weak? To help the weak is of charity; to wish to help the powerful is of elation. And the sense is: while you aim to help him under whose greatness you succumb: the comfort you offer is of ostentation, not of piety.
26.3: 26.3 To whom have you given. Ibid. To give counsel to a fool is of charity, to give counsel to the wise himself is of perversity, hence it follows: And prudence, etc. Everyone who is right in prudence is not very much: because he does not seek to know more than it behooves to know. Very much. Beyond measure, as those who wish to seem more learned than others, whence it comes that the immoderate also speak foolish things, hence the excess of prudence is added:
26.4: 26.4 Whom to teach. We live by the breath without which we have no wisdom, but through which. He therefore who gives life gives wisdom also. Breath. AUGUSTINE. As we cannot but from our nature, etc., down to because not created the created. Is it not he who. Ibid. Bildad, because Job scourged, etc., down to he expands through sentences saying: Behold the giants groan under the waters. After he repressed the swelling of wisdom, etc., down to by which he raises himself on high.
26.5: 26.5 And they that dwell with. Those who are associated with such alike groan, because they too are depressed by participation in their labor; and because desired heights cannot be administered without sins, and the evil that is done is not hidden from divine wrath.
26.6: 26.6 Hell is naked. By the name of hell and perdition he designates the devil and the companions of his whole damnation.
26.7: 26.7 Who stretches out. Ibid. By the name of the north the devil is called, who, to bind the hearts of the nations with the cold of the body, said: I will sit on the mountain of the covenant in the sides of the north. Who is stretched over the empty, because he possesses those hearts which are not possessed by the grace of divine love. And hangs the earth. Ibid. By the name of earth the Church is designated, etc., down to All nations are reckoned as nothing and vanity.
26.8: 26.8 Who binds. Ibid. He narrates the beginnings of the nascent Church saying, etc., down to lest by the immensity of it the hearers be oppressed.
26.9: 26.9 Who holds back the face. In the face knowledge is shown. The face of his throne is therefore held back, because by us in this life the glory of his kingdom is not known. Upon which he spreads his cloud, it is said, because as it is, that heavenly glory is not seen. The face of his throne. The throne is his majesty, or the angels, who now cannot be fully known; or we ourselves, whose face, that is knowledge, is forbidden to advance to higher things: over whom is the cloud, in whom he brings forth hidden judgments, hence he adds:
26.10: 26.10 He has set bounds about the waters. Because he moderates the knowledge of the human race, so that as long as the vicissitudes of alternating times pass, they do not perfectly attain to the knowledge of the inner clarity.
26.11: 26.11 The pillars. GREGORY THE GREAT. The pillars of heaven he calls the holy angels, or the highest preachers of the Church.
26.12: 26.12 By his strength. Ibid. Because the Lord incarnate, hearts at variance in the Church believe in concord. And by his wisdom. The ancient enemy was struck by wisdom, not by power, because while he boldly sought Christ, in whom nothing was his, he justly lost man, whom he also justly held. But the Lord being slain, what glory of the preacher is to follow, it follows:
26.13: 26.13 His spirit adorned the heavens. Because the preachers, unless they had received the promised gifts of the Paraclete, would have shone with no beauty of fortitude. And his hand delivering. The ancient enemy, who spoke to man by the mouth of the serpent, who is called crooked, because he did not stand in the rectitude of truth; he, by the delivering hand of the Lord, was cast out of the Church. In few sentences he related the order of the first coming of the Lord, but adds that the second is greatly to be feared.
26.14: 26.14 Lo, these are but a part of his ways. Ibid. By the name of ways, etc., down to as a thin drop of the heavenly liquor flows to us. And when we have scarcely heard a little. As if to say: If we scarcely bear the wonderful things of his humility, by what strength shall we bear the terrible coming of his majesty?
27.1: 27.1 Job added also, etc. GREGORY on Job, book 18. The Church suffers bitter things from enemies in two ways: either by words, where her wisdom is exercised; or by swords, where her patience is proved. Now of that persecution he speaks where she is provoked by false assertions.
27.2: 27.2 As God lives. There are those who, suffering adversities, believe not that God is: some think God is, but that he cares nothing for human affairs. This man, set in the type of the Church in affliction, that he may confess that God is, says: As God lives. And to declare that he cares for human affairs, he adds: Who has taken away my judgment, etc.
27.4: 27.4 My lips shall not speak. Ibid. That before iniquity, etc., down to to meditate on studious depravity.
27.5: 27.5 God forbid. Because Solomon says: He that justifies the wicked, and he that condemns the just, both are abominable before God. And this is: God forbid. For he would depart from innocence if he thought good of those evils.
27.6: 27.6 My justification. Ibid. He would abandon the justification begun, if he declined into praise of sinners. He well keeps from others who first guards himself from his own: as, therefore I fear to sin about them, because my heart does not reprove me. For my heart does not reprove me. As if to say, etc., down to yet he strongly resisted thought.
27.7: 27.7 Let my enemy be as the wicked. Ibid. The wicked is called the unbeliever, etc., down to who does not agree with me in work.
27.8: 27.8 For what is the hope of the hypocrite. The hypocrite, who in Latin is called pretender, is a covetous robber, who while doing unjustly desires to be venerated for holiness, snatches the praise of another's life.
27.9: 27.9 Will God hear? Because in judgment he finds no remedy in the cry, who now loses the fitting time of crying. Of whose depravity it is added:
27.10: 27.10 Or can he delight in the Almighty? He who is overcome by love of earthly things in no way delights in God: And call upon God at all times. The hypocrite calls upon God only when the tribulation of earthly things straitens him.
27.11: 27.11 I will teach you by the hand. The hand of God is called the Son, etc., down to it is sin to him.
27.14: 27.14 If his children be multiplied. Ibid. Those who are begotten by the preaching of heretics are struck by the sentence of the judgment to come. And his grandchildren. The grandchildren of heretics are, etc., down to he leaves some obstinate in malice. It follows:
27.15: 27.15 Those that remain of him. Of that people of heretics, namely, those left shall be buried in destruction, because while they do not return to the light of truth they are weighed down by earthly understanding. And his widows shall not weep. By widows he means the subject peoples deprived of the heretic by death: who, while the preacher of error is snatched to eternal punishments, often return to the grace of true knowledge.
27.16: 27.16 If he heap up. Ibid. Silver, that is the speech of heretics, etc., down to they weave the testimonies of Holy Scripture.
27.17: 27.17 He shall prepare indeed. Because a man full of right faith gathers the testimonies of Scripture which the heretic brings, and thence convicts the obstinacy of error, as David slew Goliath with his own sword. And the innocent shall divide the silver. To divide the silver innocent, etc., down to because they mix false things with true.
27.18: 27.18 He has built his house as a moth. Ibid. The moth builds a house for itself by corrupting: so the heretic makes the place of his perfidy only in the minds which he corrupts. And as a keeper. The shelter of the keeper, etc., down to the speech is raised up, when it is added.
27.19: 27.19 The rich man when he shall sleep. The rich man sleeps and opens his eyes, because when he dies with the flesh his soul is compelled to see what he scorned to foresee.
27.20: 27.20 Poverty shall lay hold on him. For in hell, want working, the burning rich man was compelled to ask even the smallest things, who here, avarice working, came to deny the least things. The night shall oppress him. By night he calls the hidden time of sudden departure, by the name of tempest he designates the whirlwind of judgment.
